FILE: Nutrient Database/Dietary Carbohydrates/insoluble-bulking-fiber.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Insoluble Bulking Fiber"
description: "Insoluble bulking fibre — cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin and wheat bran: how it speeds transit and adds stool bulk, food sources and practical cautions."
slug: "Insoluble Bulking Fiber"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Dietary Carbohydrates"
seoKeywords: ["insoluble fibre", "wheat bran", "cellulose", "lignin", "constipation", "stool bulk", "transit time"]
tags: ["fiber", "carbohydrate", "gut-health"]
---

## Overview

Insoluble fibre is the structural material of plant cell walls — principally **cellulose**, **hemicellulose** and **lignin**, along with resistant starch fractions in some foods. It does not dissolve in water, is only slowly and partially fermented by colonic bacteria, and passes through the gut largely intact.

## Why it matters

**Bulk and transit.** Insoluble fibre holds water within its structure rather than forming a gel, increasing stool mass and softening consistency. Larger, softer stool distends the colon and stimulates peristalsis, shortening transit time. This is the mechanism behind wheat bran's long-standing use for constipation, and the reason it is the fibre type most reliably associated with improved bowel regularity.

**Dilution and binding.** By increasing faecal bulk and reducing transit time, insoluble fibre lowers the concentration of luminal contents and shortens the period of mucosal contact. This is one of the proposed mechanisms behind the observed association between higher whole-grain and fibre intake and lower colorectal cancer risk, although the evidence is observational and the causal picture is not settled.

**Metabolic effects are modest.** Unlike viscous soluble fibre, insoluble fibre has little effect on LDL cholesterol and only a limited effect on post-meal glucose. Its contribution to satiety comes mainly from the chewing and volume of the whole foods that carry it.

**Lignin** is technically not a carbohydrate but a complex polyphenolic polymer; it is grouped with fibre because it is indigestible and structurally bound into plant cell walls.

## Recommended intake

Recommendations are for total dietary fibre rather than for insoluble fibre separately: the Institute of Medicine Adequate Intake is 14 g per 1,000 kcal, which works out to roughly 25 g/day for adult women and 38 g/day for adult men. Whole foods supply a mixture of soluble and insoluble fractions, which is the sensible way to meet the target.

## Food sources

Wheat bran and whole wheat, brown rice and other intact whole grains, the skins and peels of fruit and vegetables, cauliflower, green beans, potatoes with skin, nuts and seeds, and legumes.

## Practical cautions

- Increase intake gradually and **with adequate fluid**. Bulking fibre without enough water can worsen rather than relieve constipation.
- Wheat bran can aggravate symptoms in some people with irritable bowel syndrome; soluble fibres such as psyllium are usually better tolerated in that group.
- Insoluble fibre from bran binds minerals such as iron, zinc and calcium to a degree, mainly through associated phytate. This matters most for people with marginal mineral intakes.
- Anyone with a known bowel stricture, obstruction or severe motility disorder should not increase bulking fibre without medical advice.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Dietary Carbohydrates/soluble-viscous-fiber.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Soluble Viscous Fiber"
description: "Soluble viscous fibre — beta-glucan, pectin, psyllium and guar: how viscosity lowers cholesterol and blunts glucose, fermentation to SCFAs, and food sources."
slug: "Soluble Viscous Fiber"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Dietary Carbohydrates"
seoKeywords: ["soluble fibre", "viscous fibre", "beta-glucan", "psyllium", "pectin", "cholesterol", "short-chain fatty acids"]
tags: ["fiber", "carbohydrate", "gut-health"]
---

## Overview

Dietary fibre is carbohydrate that human digestive enzymes cannot break down. The traditional soluble/insoluble split is a simplification, but it remains useful because the fibres that dissolve in water and form a **viscous gel** behave very differently from those that do not.

Viscous soluble fibres include beta-glucan (oats, barley), pectin (apples, citrus, guava), psyllium husk (isabgol), guar gum, glucomannan and the mucilage in okra, flaxseed and chia.

## Why it matters

**Viscosity is the mechanism.** A gel in the small intestine slows gastric emptying and creates an unstirred layer that delays contact between nutrients and the mucosa. Three consequences follow:

1. **Blood glucose.** Slower carbohydrate delivery flattens the post-meal glucose and insulin rise. This is a well-established effect and part of why oats and legumes have low glycaemic responses.
2. **Cholesterol.** The gel traps bile acids and carries them out in the stool. The liver must then draw on circulating cholesterol to synthesise replacements, lowering LDL cholesterol. The effect of oat beta-glucan and psyllium on LDL is one of the better-substantiated diet-lipid relationships and is the basis of approved health claims in several jurisdictions.
3. **Satiety.** Increased gastric distension and slower emptying prolong fullness, though the effect on body weight in trials is modest.

**Fermentation.** Colonic bacteria ferment most soluble fibres to short-chain fatty acids — acetate, propionate and butyrate. Butyrate is the preferred fuel of colonocytes and has been shown in laboratory work to support barrier integrity and modulate inflammation. Fermentation also produces gas, which is why a sudden large increase in soluble fibre causes bloating; increasing intake gradually and with adequate fluid avoids most of this.

Not all soluble fibres are viscous. Inulin, fructo-oligosaccharides and partially hydrolysed guar gum dissolve but do not gel; they are highly fermentable prebiotics and act mainly on the microbiota rather than on glucose or lipids.

## Recommended intake

Fibre intake recommendations cover total fibre rather than soluble fibre separately. The Adequate Intake set by the Institute of Medicine is 14 g of total fibre per 1,000 kcal — roughly 25 g/day for adult women and 38 g/day for adult men. Most people fall well short.

## Food sources

Oats and oat bran, barley, psyllium husk, legumes and lentils, apples, guava, oranges and other citrus, carrots, okra, flaxseed and chia seed, and bananas.

## A practical caution

Viscous fibres can slow the absorption of medication taken at the same time. Psyllium and similar preparations should be taken with plenty of water and separated from medicines by a couple of hours. People with strictures or significantly impaired gut motility should seek medical advice before using bulking preparations.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Dietary Supplement Fact Sheets](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Energy Content by Food Category/ndb-cal-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Calorie Database: Energy Density, Atwater Factors & the Complete kcal Reference by Food"
description: "How food energy is measured and labelled: Atwater factors, energy density, why label calories are estimates, and how energy varies across food categories."
slug: "ndb-cal-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Energy Content by Food Category"
seoKeywords: ["calories", "atwater factors", "energy density", "kcal", "food labels", "kilojoules", "metabolisable energy"]
tags: ["energy", "reference", "macronutrient"]
---

## Overview

A food calorie is a kilocalorie (kcal): the energy needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of water by one degree Celsius. Many countries label in kilojoules instead — **1 kcal = 4.184 kJ**.

## How the numbers are produced

Food energy on labels and in databases is almost never measured directly for that product. It is **calculated** from macronutrient content using the **Atwater general factors**:

| Component | kcal per gram |
| :--- | ---: |
| Carbohydrate (available) | 4 |
| Protein | 4 |
| Fat | 9 |
| Alcohol | 7 |
| Organic acids | 3 |
| Polyols (sugar alcohols) | ~2.4 |
| Fibre | ~2 |

These are **metabolisable energy** values — gross combustion energy minus losses in faeces and urine — averaged across mixed diets in early twentieth-century experiments. USDA also maintains food-specific Atwater factors for some categories, which give somewhat different results than the general factors.

## Why label calories are approximations

Several well-documented effects mean the number on the packet is an estimate, not a measurement:

- **Food matrix.** Energy from whole almonds and pistachios is measurably lower than Atwater predicts, because intact cell walls prevent complete fat release during digestion. Grinding into nut butter closes much of that gap.
- **Processing and cooking.** Cooking gelatinises starch and denatures protein, increasing digestibility and therefore available energy. Highly processed food is generally more completely absorbed than the same nutrients in whole-food form.
- **Fibre and fermentation.** Energy recovered from colonic fermentation of fibre and resistant starch varies with the individual's microbiota.
- **Thermic effect of food.** Protein costs roughly 20–30% of its own energy to digest and metabolise, carbohydrate around 5–10%, fat around 0–3%. Net energy from a high-protein meal is therefore lower than its gross calorie count implies.
- **Labelling tolerances.** Most regulators permit a margin of error on declared values, commonly around 20%.

None of this makes calorie counting useless; it makes precision beyond a rough band unjustified.

## Energy density

Energy density is kcal per gram of food, and it is driven mostly by water and fat content. Roughly:

| Category | Typical energy density |
| :--- | :--- |
| Non-starchy vegetables, most fruit, broths | Very low (well under 1 kcal/g) |
| Cooked grains, pulses, potatoes, curd, lean fish | Low to medium |
| Bread, cheese, fatty meat, dried fruit | Medium to high |
| Nuts, seeds, chocolate, biscuits, fried snacks | High |
| Oils, ghee, butter | Highest (around 9 kcal/g) |

Because people tend to eat a fairly consistent *weight* of food from day to day, lowering the average energy density of the diet — more vegetables, fruit, pulses and broth-based dishes — reduces energy intake without reducing the volume of food eaten. This is one of the better-supported practical strategies in weight management.

## Using calorie data sensibly

- Compare foods **per 100 g**, not per serving; serving sizes are chosen by manufacturers.
- Cooking changes weight substantially. Check whether a database entry refers to raw or cooked food — 100 g of raw rice and 100 g of cooked rice are very different things.
- Added cooking fat is frequently the largest uncounted contributor to a home-cooked meal's energy.
- Beverages, including juice and alcohol, contribute energy with little satiety.
- Energy needs vary widely with body size, composition, age and activity; predictive equations carry meaningful error, and observed weight change over a few weeks is a better guide than any calculator.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [FAO — Food energy: methods of analysis and conversion factors](https://www.fao.org/4/y5022e/y5022e00.htm)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss weight and dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Essential Amino Acids/branched-chain-amino-acids.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Branched Chain Amino Acids"
description: "BCAAs — leucine, isoleucine and valine: muscle metabolism, leucine and mTOR signalling, food sources, and what the evidence does and doesn't support."
slug: "Branched Chain Amino Acids"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Essential Amino Acids"
seoKeywords: ["bcaa", "leucine", "isoleucine", "valine", "muscle protein synthesis", "mtor", "whey protein"]
tags: ["amino-acid", "protein", "essential-nutrient"]
---

## Overview

The branched-chain amino acids — **leucine**, **isoleucine** and **valine** — are three of the nine essential amino acids, named for their branched aliphatic side chains. They are distinctive in that they are metabolised largely in skeletal muscle rather than in the liver.

## Why they matter

**Muscle protein synthesis.** Leucine is not only a substrate but a signal: it activates the mTORC1 pathway, which switches on the machinery of protein synthesis. A meal must supply enough leucine to cross this activation threshold for a robust anabolic response — the basis of the "leucine trigger" concept in sports and clinical nutrition, and one reason protein distribution across meals is discussed in older adults, in whom the response to leucine is blunted (anabolic resistance).

**Energy metabolism.** Because muscle expresses branched-chain aminotransferase, BCAAs can be transaminated and oxidised locally for energy during prolonged exercise. Isoleucine and valine are glucogenic; leucine is ketogenic.

**Clinical relevance.** Maple syrup urine disease is an inherited defect in BCAA catabolism requiring strict dietary restriction. BCAA-enriched formulations have been used in hepatic encephalopathy, with modest and debated benefit. In the other direction, elevated plasma BCAAs are consistently associated with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk — though whether this is causal or a marker of disturbed metabolism remains unresolved.

## What supplements do and don't do

Isolated BCAA supplements are among the best-selling sports products, and the evidence for them is weaker than the marketing suggests. Muscle protein synthesis requires **all** the essential amino acids; supplying three of them without the other six raises signalling but cannot sustain synthesis, and controlled studies generally find isolated BCAAs inferior to a complete protein such as whey. For anyone already meeting protein requirements from food, added BCAAs offer little. Claims for reduced muscle soreness and reduced fatigue are inconsistent across trials.

The practical conclusion: prioritise adequate total protein of good quality, spread across the day. Whole protein foods deliver BCAAs alongside everything else needed.

## Food sources

Whey and casein (dairy proteins are particularly leucine-rich), eggs, chicken, fish, beef, soy and tofu, lentils and other pulses, peanuts, pumpkin seeds and quinoa.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central — amino acid composition data](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/ExerciseAndAthleticPerformance-HealthProfessional/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Essential Amino Acids/l-lysine.md
========================================================================
---
title: "L Lysine"
description: "L-lysine: an essential amino acid for collagen cross-linking and carnitine synthesis, why it limits cereal protein quality, and its food sources."
slug: "L Lysine"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Essential Amino Acids"
seoKeywords: ["l-lysine", "essential amino acid", "limiting amino acid", "collagen", "carnitine", "protein quality", "food sources"]
tags: ["amino-acid", "protein", "essential-nutrient"]
---

## Overview

Lysine is one of the nine indispensable (essential) amino acids — the body cannot synthesise it and must obtain it from dietary protein. It is a basic, positively charged amino acid, and it holds a special place in nutrition because it is the **limiting amino acid** in cereal grains.

## Why it matters

**Collagen and connective tissue.** Lysine residues in collagen are hydroxylated by a vitamin C-dependent enzyme and then cross-linked by the copper-dependent enzyme lysyl oxidase. These cross-links are what give collagen and elastin their tensile strength, so lysine sits alongside vitamin C and copper in connective tissue integrity.

**Carnitine synthesis.** Lysine, with methionine, vitamin C, iron, niacin and vitamin B6, is a precursor of carnitine, which shuttles long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for oxidation.

**Protein synthesis and regulation.** Lysine residues are prime sites for post-translational modification — acetylation, methylation, ubiquitination — making them central to gene regulation and protein turnover. Lysine is also required for calcium absorption and normal growth.

**Protein quality.** Wheat, rice, maize and other cereals are relatively low in lysine, while legumes and pulses are comparatively rich in it and low in methionine. This complementarity is the biochemical basis for the grain-and-pulse combinations that appear independently in cuisines worldwide — dal with rice or roti, beans with tortilla, hummus with bread. Protein quality scoring systems (PDCAAS, DIAAS) frequently identify lysine as the limiting amino acid in cereal-based diets.

**Deficiency** does not occur in isolation in people eating enough total protein; it is a feature of overall protein-energy undernutrition, particularly in diets heavily dominated by a single cereal.

## Food sources

Meat, poultry, fish and eggs; dairy, particularly curd, paneer and cheese; soy and soy products; lentils, rajma, chana and other pulses; pumpkin seeds; and quinoa and amaranth, which are unusually lysine-rich for seed crops.

## On lysine supplements

Lysine supplements are widely sold for recurrent herpes simplex (cold sores). The trials that exist are small, older and inconsistent, and the evidence is not strong enough to support a confident recommendation. High-dose supplementation is not necessary for anyone meeting protein requirements from food, and should be discussed with a clinician, particularly by people with kidney disease.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central — amino acid composition data](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Dietary Supplement Fact Sheets](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Essential Amino Acids/l-tryptophan.md
========================================================================
---
title: "L Tryptophan"
description: "L-tryptophan: precursor of serotonin, melatonin and niacin, how it competes for brain transport, food sources, and an honest view of supplements."
slug: "L Tryptophan"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Essential Amino Acids"
seoKeywords: ["l-tryptophan", "serotonin", "melatonin", "niacin", "5-htp", "essential amino acid", "food sources"]
tags: ["amino-acid", "protein", "essential-nutrient"]
---

## Overview

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid and the least abundant of the twenty in dietary protein. Beyond its role as a protein building block, it is the precursor for two important signalling molecules and for a vitamin.

## Why it matters

**Serotonin and melatonin.** Tryptophan is hydroxylated to 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) and then decarboxylated to serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood, appetite, sleep and gut motility. Most of the body's serotonin is actually made in the gut. In the pineal gland serotonin is further converted to melatonin, the hormone that signals darkness and regulates the sleep-wake cycle.

**Niacin.** Via the kynurenine pathway, tryptophan can be converted to nicotinamide and thus contribute to vitamin B3 status — roughly 60 mg of tryptophan yields about 1 mg of niacin equivalent. This is why niacin requirements are expressed in niacin equivalents, and why pellagra appears in populations eating maize-based diets low in both niacin and tryptophan.

**Brain uptake is competitive.** Tryptophan crosses the blood-brain barrier on the large neutral amino acid transporter, competing with leucine, isoleucine, valine, tyrosine and phenylalanine. Because a protein-rich meal raises all of these together, eating turkey — or any high-protein food — does not straightforwardly raise brain tryptophan. A carbohydrate-containing meal triggers insulin, which drives the branched-chain amino acids into muscle and leaves tryptophan relatively more available for transport. This is a real mechanism, but its practical effect on mood or sleepiness from ordinary meals is modest and easily overstated.

## Food sources

Tryptophan is present in essentially all protein foods: eggs, milk and cheese, chicken and turkey, fish, soy and tofu, pumpkin and sesame seeds, peanuts, oats and lentils. Per gram of protein the differences between sources are small; total protein intake matters more than food choice.

## On supplements

Tryptophan and 5-HTP supplements are marketed for sleep and low mood. Evidence is limited and inconsistent. More importantly, there are genuine safety considerations: combining these with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAO inhibitors, triptans or tramadol raises the risk of serotonin syndrome. A contaminated batch of tryptophan supplements was also linked to an outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome in 1989, which led to regulatory restrictions in several countries. Anyone considering these products, especially alongside psychiatric medication, should speak to a clinician first.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central — amino acid composition data](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Niacin Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Niacin-HealthProfessional/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Essential Fatty Acids/alpha-linolenic-acid.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Alpha Linolenic Acid"
description: "Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, 18:3 n-3): the essential plant omega-3, its limited conversion to EPA and DHA, adult AI values, and food sources like flax and walnut."
slug: "Alpha Linolenic Acid"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Essential Fatty Acids"
seoKeywords: ["alpha-linolenic acid", "ala", "plant omega-3", "flaxseed", "conversion to epa", "adequate intake", "chia"]
tags: ["fatty-acid", "omega-3", "essential-nutrient"]
---

## Overview

Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) is an 18-carbon fatty acid with three double bonds, the first at the omega-3 position. It is one of the two essential fatty acids humans cannot synthesise, and it is the omega-3 found in plants.

## Why it matters

ALA serves as a membrane component and an energy substrate in its own right, but much of the interest in it concerns its role as the parent of the long-chain omega-3s **EPA** (eicosapentaenoic acid) and **DHA** (docosahexaenoic acid), which carry out most of the physiological functions attributed to omega-3 fats — membrane fluidity in neural and retinal tissue, precursor supply for resolvins and protectins, and effects on triglycerides and platelet function.

**Conversion is limited.** The elongation and desaturation of ALA to EPA is inefficient in humans, and onward conversion to DHA more so. Reported conversion efficiencies vary widely between studies and between individuals, but all agree it is low; women of reproductive age convert somewhat better than men, likely an oestrogen effect. Conversion is further suppressed by high linoleic acid intake, because both fatty acid families compete for the same delta-6 desaturase.

The practical implication: ALA-rich foods are valuable and are associated with cardiovascular benefit in observational studies, but people who eat no fish or seafood should not assume flaxseed will supply their DHA. An algal oil supplement is the reliable vegetarian route to preformed DHA, and is worth considering in pregnancy and lactation.

## Recommended intake

There is no RDA; Adequate Intakes are set.

| Group | Amount per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Men 19+ | 1.6 g |
| Women 19+ | 1.1 g |
| Pregnancy | 1.4 g |
| Lactation | 1.3 g |

No Tolerable Upper Intake Level has been established.

## Food sources

Flaxseed and flaxseed (linseed) oil are the most concentrated common sources; also chia seeds, walnuts, hemp seeds, canola/rapeseed oil, mustard oil, soybean oil, perilla oil, and, in smaller amounts, leafy greens and legumes.

**Storage matters.** Highly unsaturated oils oxidise readily. Flax and chia are best bought fresh, ground shortly before use (whole flaxseed passes through undigested), and kept cool and dark. Rancid oil is not merely unpalatable — oxidised lipids are undesirable.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Omega-3 Fatty Acids Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Omega3FattyAcids-HealthProfessional/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Essential Fatty Acids/eicosapentaenoic-and-docosahexaenoic-acid.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Eicosapentaenoic And Docosahexaenoic Acid"
description: "EPA and DHA: distinct roles in triglycerides, inflammation resolution and brain and retinal function, dietary sources, supplement forms and safety."
slug: "Eicosapentaenoic And Docosahexaenoic Acid"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Essential Fatty Acids"
seoKeywords: ["epa", "dha", "long-chain omega-3", "fish oil", "algal oil", "triglycerides", "brain development"]
tags: ["fatty-acid", "omega-3", "micronutrient"]
---

## Overview

EPA (20:5 n-3) and DHA (22:6 n-3) are the long-chain omega-3 fatty acids. They can be made from alpha-linolenic acid, but only inefficiently, so dietary intake largely determines tissue levels. They are not formally classed as essential nutrients — but they behave, functionally, like ones.

## Why they matter

**DHA is structural.** It is highly concentrated in the phospholipids of the brain grey matter and the retinal photoreceptor outer segments, where its flexible, highly unsaturated chain supports membrane fluidity and the conformational changes rhodopsin undergoes during phototransduction. DHA accretion in the fetal brain and retina is greatest in the third trimester and the first two years of life, which is why maternal and infant DHA supply receives attention.

**EPA is predominantly a signalling molecule.** It competes with arachidonic acid as an eicosanoid substrate, producing less inflammatory 3-series prostaglandins and 5-series leukotrienes, and it is the precursor of E-series resolvins — specialised mediators that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely suppressing it. DHA yields D-series resolvins and protectins.

**Where the clinical evidence is strongest:** high-dose omega-3 reliably lowers serum triglycerides, a dose-dependent and well-replicated effect, and prescription preparations are licensed for hypertriglyceridaemia. Regular fish consumption is consistently associated with lower cardiovascular mortality.

**Where it is weaker or mixed:** large trials of general-population omega-3 supplementation for prevention of cardiovascular events have produced mixed results, and evidence for cognition, depression and inflammatory joint disease is inconsistent. High-dose supplements have also been associated with a small increase in atrial fibrillation risk in some trials. Fish as a food and fish oil as a supplement should not be assumed equivalent.

## Recommended intake

No RDA or Adequate Intake has been set for EPA and DHA specifically; the DRI for omega-3 is expressed as ALA. Most cardiovascular guidelines instead recommend eating **two servings of fish per week**, at least one of them oily. Therapeutic doses for hypertriglyceridaemia are considerably higher and belong under medical supervision.

## Food sources and supplement forms

Oily fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring, anchovies, hilsa, rawas and trout — are the richest dietary sources; shellfish and lean white fish contribute smaller amounts. For vegetarians and vegans, **algal oil** supplies preformed DHA (and increasingly EPA) from the microalgae that fish acquire it from in the first place.

Supplements come as triglycerides, re-esterified triglycerides and ethyl esters; absorption differs somewhat, and taking them with a fat-containing meal improves uptake in all cases. Krill oil supplies phospholipid-bound omega-3 at generally lower doses per capsule.

## Safety and interactions

- Fishy aftertaste, belching and loose stools are the common complaints; freezing capsules or taking them with meals helps.
- High doses may prolong bleeding time; discuss with a clinician if you take anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs or have surgery planned.
- Choose products tested for oxidation and contaminants. Pregnant women are advised to limit high-mercury fish such as king mackerel, shark, swordfish and tilefish while still eating low-mercury fish.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Omega-3 Fatty Acids Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Omega3FattyAcids-HealthProfessional/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*

FILE: Nutrient Database/Essential Fatty Acids/linoleic-acid.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Linoleic Acid"
description: "Linoleic acid (LA, 18:2 n-6): the essential omega-6 fatty acid, its role in skin barrier and arachidonic acid synthesis, adult AI values and food sources."
slug: "Linoleic Acid"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Essential Fatty Acids"
seoKeywords: ["linoleic acid", "omega-6", "essential fatty acid", "arachidonic acid", "adequate intake", "vegetable oils"]
tags: ["fatty-acid", "omega-6", "essential-nutrient"]
---

## Overview

Linoleic acid (LA) is an 18-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid with two double bonds, the first at the omega-6 position. Humans lack the desaturase enzymes needed to place a double bond beyond carbon 9, so linoleic acid — like alpha-linolenic acid — must come from the diet. These two are the only truly essential fatty acids.

## Why it matters

**Skin barrier.** Linoleic acid is incorporated into ceramides in the stratum corneum, where it is indispensable for a water-tight epidermal barrier. The earliest and most specific sign of essential fatty acid deficiency is a scaly dermatitis with increased transepidermal water loss.

**Membrane structure.** As a component of phospholipids, LA contributes to membrane fluidity and to the function of membrane-bound receptors and transporters.

**Eicosanoid precursor.** LA is elongated and desaturated to arachidonic acid, the substrate for prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes that regulate inflammation, platelet aggregation, vascular tone and immune signalling. The same desaturase enzymes act on omega-3 fatty acids, so the two families compete — the basis of longstanding interest in the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio.

**Clinical deficiency** is rare in people eating ordinary diets and is seen mainly with prolonged fat-free parenteral nutrition or severe fat malabsorption.

## On the omega-6 debate

Linoleic acid intake has risen substantially in most countries with the increased use of seed oils, and it is often blamed for chronic inflammation. The honest position is that this is contested. Controlled feeding studies show that raising dietary LA does not reliably increase tissue arachidonic acid or systemic inflammatory markers, and pooled observational data generally associate higher linoleic acid intake with **lower**, not higher, cardiovascular risk. What is better supported is the value of increasing omega-3 intake rather than aggressively cutting omega-6, and of replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat overall.

## Recommended intake

There is no RDA; Adequate Intakes are set.

| Group | Amount per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Men 19–50 | 17 g |
| Men 51+ | 14 g |
| Women 19–50 | 12 g |
| Women 51+ | 11 g |
| Pregnancy | 13 g |
| Lactation | 13 g |

The Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range for total fat is 20–35% of energy.

## Food sources

Safflower, sunflower, corn, soybean, cottonseed, sesame and groundnut oils; walnuts, sunflower seeds, pine nuts, almonds and peanuts; and, in smaller amounts, poultry and eggs.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Omega-3 Fatty Acids Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Omega3FattyAcids-HealthProfessional/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Fatty Acid Biochemistry & Health/oil-nutr-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Plant Fatty Acid Biochemistry: Saturated, MUFA, PUFA, Omega-3:6 Ratios, Trans Fats & Metabolic Health"
description: "How fatty acid structure determines function: chain length, saturation and cis/trans geometry, the omega-3:6 ratio debate, trans fats, and what this means for cooking oils."
slug: "oil-nutr-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Fatty Acid Biochemistry & Health"
seoKeywords: ["fatty acid structure", "saturated fat", "mufa", "pufa", "trans fat", "omega-3 to omega-6 ratio", "smoke point"]
tags: ["fatty-acid", "lipids", "biochemistry"]
---

## Overview

Every dietary fat is a mixture of fatty acids, and the behaviour of a fat — in the pan and in the body — follows from three structural features: **chain length**, **degree of saturation**, and **double-bond geometry**.

## The structural variables

**Chain length.** Short-chain fatty acids (up to 5 carbons) are mostly produced by colonic fermentation of fibre rather than eaten. Medium-chain fatty acids (6–12 carbons, abundant in coconut and palm kernel oil) are absorbed directly into the portal circulation and reach the liver without needing carnitine-dependent transport. Long-chain fatty acids (14+ carbons) dominate the diet and are packaged into chylomicrons.

**Saturation.** Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds; their straight chains pack tightly, so they are solid at room temperature and chemically stable. Monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA) have one double bond, polyunsaturated (PUFA) two or more. Each cis double bond introduces a kink that prevents tight packing — hence liquid oils — and each is a site vulnerable to oxidation. This is the central trade-off: **the more unsaturated an oil, the more biologically interesting and the less chemically stable it is.**

**Geometry.** Naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids are almost all *cis*. **Trans** fatty acids have the hydrogens on opposite sides, straightening the chain so it behaves more like a saturated fat.

## Naming conventions

Notation such as 18:2 n-6 reads as: 18 carbons, 2 double bonds, first double bond 6 carbons from the methyl (omega) end. The omega position is what defines a fatty acid family, and families are not interconvertible in humans — omega-6 cannot become omega-3.

## Trans fats

Industrial partial hydrogenation was used to solidify liquid oils for margarine, bakery shortening and vanaspati. The resulting trans fats raise LDL cholesterol, lower HDL cholesterol, and are associated with increased cardiovascular risk more strongly than any other fat type. The evidence was consistent enough that the WHO called for global elimination and many countries have now banned or capped industrial trans fats. Small amounts of naturally occurring ruminant trans fats (in dairy and beef) appear to behave differently and are not the target of these policies.

Repeatedly reheated frying oil also generates trans isomers and oxidation products — a real concern in commercial deep-frying.

## The omega-6 to omega-3 ratio

Omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids compete for the same desaturase and elongase enzymes and give rise to eicosanoids with differing signalling properties, which led to the proposal that a high dietary ratio drives chronic inflammation. It is a plausible mechanism and a genuinely useful teaching model, but it has been oversold. Controlled feeding studies find that raising linoleic acid does not consistently raise tissue arachidonic acid or inflammatory markers, and prospective cohort data generally associate higher linoleic acid intake with lower cardiovascular risk. The better-supported practical message is to **increase omega-3 intake** rather than to chase a numerical ratio.

## What this means for cooking oils

- Match the oil to the method. Oils high in MUFA and saturated fat (mustard, groundnut, rice bran, ghee, refined olive) tolerate heat better than highly polyunsaturated oils (flax, walnut, unrefined sunflower).
- Refining raises smoke point; unrefined and cold-pressed oils carry more phenolics but smoke sooner.
- Do not reuse frying oil repeatedly, and discard oil that has darkened, thickened or smells acrid.
- Variety across the week is more useful than searching for one perfect oil.
- Overall, replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat — rather than with refined carbohydrate — is the substitution with the best evidence behind it.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [World Health Organization — Trans fat](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trans-fat)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Omega-3 Fatty Acids Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Omega3FattyAcids-HealthProfessional/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Fatty Acids & Lipids/ndb-fat-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Fat Database: Saturated, MUFA, PUFA, Omega-3, Omega-6 & the Complete Fatty Acid Reference"
description: "A reference guide to dietary fat: the fatty acid classes, cholesterol and lipoproteins, how to read fat on a nutrition label, and where each fat type is found."
slug: "ndb-fat-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Fatty Acids & Lipids"
seoKeywords: ["dietary fat", "saturated fat", "mufa", "pufa", "omega-3", "omega-6", "cholesterol", "nutrition label"]
tags: ["lipids", "macronutrient", "reference"]
---

## Overview

"Fat" on a food label refers almost entirely to triglycerides — three fatty acids esterified to a glycerol backbone. Fats supply about 9 kcal per gram, carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, provide the two essential fatty acids, and form the phospholipid membranes of every cell. No food fat is a single fatty acid; every one is a blend, and describing an oil as "a saturated fat" or "a monounsaturated fat" is shorthand for whichever class predominates.

## The fatty acid classes

**Saturated fatty acids (SFA)** — no double bonds. Common members include palmitic (16:0), stearic (18:0), myristic (14:0) and lauric (12:0) acid. Found in ghee, butter, cheese, fatty cuts of meat, coconut and palm oil. They are not interchangeable in their effect on blood lipids: lauric, myristic and palmitic acid raise LDL cholesterol, while stearic acid appears broadly neutral. Most guidelines recommend limiting saturated fat to under about 10% of energy, on the strength of the LDL and substitution evidence.

**Monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA)** — one double bond; principally oleic acid (18:1 n-9). Olive oil, groundnut oil, mustard oil, canola, avocado, almonds and cashews.

**Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)** — two or more double bonds, split into two non-interconvertible families:
- **Omega-6**, headed by linoleic acid (18:2 n-6), which is essential, and elongated to arachidonic acid. Found in sunflower, safflower, corn, soybean, sesame and cottonseed oil, and in nuts and seeds.
- **Omega-3**, headed by alpha-linolenic acid (18:3 n-3), also essential, and its long-chain derivatives EPA (20:5 n-3) and DHA (22:6 n-3). ALA comes from flax, chia, walnut, hemp, canola and mustard oil; EPA and DHA from oily fish, seafood and algal oil.

**Trans fatty acids** — unsaturated fats with trans geometry. Industrially produced trans fat, from partial hydrogenation, raises LDL and lowers HDL cholesterol and is the fat most strongly linked to cardiovascular risk; global elimination is a WHO objective and many countries now restrict it. Small amounts occur naturally in ruminant dairy and meat and appear to behave differently.

**Medium-chain triglycerides (MCT)** — 6 to 12 carbons, from coconut and palm kernel oil. Absorbed via the portal vein and oxidised readily. Genuinely useful in specific malabsorption and ketogenic contexts; the broader metabolic claims made for them are not well supported.

## Dietary cholesterol and lipoproteins

Cholesterol is a sterol, not a fatty acid. It is found only in animal foods and is also synthesised endogenously, with production down-regulated when intake rises. For most people, dietary cholesterol has a smaller effect on blood cholesterol than saturated and trans fat do, and several national guidelines have dropped a specific numeric limit while still advising moderation.

Because lipids are not water-soluble, they travel in lipoproteins: chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the gut, VLDL carries endogenous triglyceride from the liver, LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues and is the main atherogenic particle, and HDL participates in reverse cholesterol transport.

## Recommended intake

- **Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range for total fat:** 20–35% of daily energy for adults.
- **Linoleic acid (AI):** 17 g/day for men 19–50 and 14 g/day for men 51+; 12 g/day for women 19–50 and 11 g/day for women 51+.
- **Alpha-linolenic acid (AI):** 1.6 g/day for men and 1.1 g/day for women aged 19+.
- **Saturated fat:** as low as practical while eating a nutritionally adequate diet; commonly capped at 10% of energy.
- **Trans fat:** as low as possible.

## Reading a nutrition label

Total fat is broken down into saturated and, in many markets, trans fat; monounsaturated and polyunsaturated are often optional. Compare products per 100 g rather than per serving, since serving sizes vary. Ingredient lists still worth scanning for partially hydrogenated oils in markets where they are not yet banned. Note that "cholesterol-free" on a vegetable oil is true of every vegetable oil and tells you nothing useful.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [World Health Organization — Trans fat](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trans-fat)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Omega-3 Fatty Acids Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Omega3FattyAcids-HealthProfessional/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Monounsaturated & Polyunsaturated Fat Sources/func-fat-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Avocado, Olive Oil, Nuts & Seeds: Monounsaturated Fats, Oleic Acid & Heart Health"
description: "Whole-food sources of monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fat — avocado, olives, nuts and seeds: what they contribute beyond oleic acid, and how to use them."
slug: "func-fat-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Monounsaturated & Polyunsaturated Fat Sources"
seoKeywords: ["monounsaturated fat", "oleic acid", "avocado", "olive oil", "nuts", "seeds", "heart health", "unsaturated fat"]
tags: ["lipids", "whole-foods", "cardiovascular"]
---

## Overview

Monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA) have a single double bond; **oleic acid (18:1 n-9)** is by far the most common in the diet. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) have two or more. Neither is an essential nutrient in the strict sense — the body can make oleic acid — but foods rich in them are among the most consistently favourable in the diet.

## What the whole foods contribute

**Olives and olive oil.** Predominantly oleic acid. Extra-virgin oil additionally carries phenolic compounds — hydroxytyrosol, oleuropein, oleocanthal — that are stripped out during refining and that account for the peppery catch at the back of the throat in a good oil.

**Avocado.** Also oleic-acid dominant, with the advantage of arriving as a whole food: substantial fibre, potassium, folate, vitamin K and lutein come with it. Avocado fat also improves absorption of carotenoids from the same meal, a useful reason to add it to salads.

**Nuts.** Almonds, hazelnuts, cashews, pistachios, macadamia and pecans are MUFA-rich; walnuts stand apart as the tree nut highest in ALA; peanuts (botanically a legume) sit in the MUFA group. All bring protein, fibre, vitamin E, magnesium, arginine and polyphenols. Nut consumption is one of the more consistent dietary correlates of lower cardiovascular risk in cohort studies, and the **PREDIMED** randomised trial included a mixed-nuts arm that showed benefit as part of a Mediterranean dietary pattern.

**Seeds.** Sunflower and sesame seeds are rich in linoleic acid and vitamin E; pumpkin seeds add magnesium and zinc; flax and chia supply ALA; hemp seeds provide a balanced PUFA profile plus complete protein.

## Why the whole-food form matters

Cohort evidence for nuts, seeds, olives and avocado is stronger and more consistent than for extracted oils. Several reasons are plausible: fibre and protein blunt the energy density, the food matrix limits how much fat is actually absorbed from chewed nuts, and micronutrients and polyphenols travel with the fat. Whichever mechanism dominates, the practical implication is the same — **prefer the food to the oil where the recipe allows.**

## Practical use

- A daily handful of mixed nuts is a well-supported, low-effort habit; choose unsalted and unsweetened.
- Use extra-virgin olive oil where its flavour survives — dressings, drizzles, gentle sautéing.
- Nuts and seeds go rancid. Buy in quantities you will finish, and refrigerate or freeze the rest.
- Toasting seeds briefly improves flavour and digestibility; heavy roasting degrades the oils.
- These foods are energy-dense. They are excellent additions to a diet, and in place of less useful fats — not simply on top of everything else.
- Nut allergy is common and can be severe; sesame is also a major allergen in many countries.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [World Health Organization — Healthy diet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/healthy-diet)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Protein, Carbohydrates & Fats/ndb-macro-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Macronutrients: Protein, Carbs & Fats — RDAs, Acceptable Ranges & the Foundation of Human Nutrition"
description: "The three macronutrients explained: energy yields, protein RDA of 0.8 g/kg, carbohydrate RDA of 130 g, fat ranges, AMDRs, and how to think about macro distribution."
slug: "ndb-macro-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Protein, Carbohydrates & Fats"
seoKeywords: ["macronutrients", "protein rda", "carbohydrate rda", "amdr", "energy yield", "dietary reference intakes"]
tags: ["macronutrient", "reference", "protein", "carbohydrate", "fat"]
---

## Overview

Macronutrients are the three classes of nutrient that supply energy: **protein**, **carbohydrate** and **fat**. Alcohol supplies energy too but is not a nutrient. Water, vitamins and minerals are essential but energy-free.

| Macronutrient | Energy yield |
| :--- | ---: |
| Carbohydrate | 4 kcal/g |
| Protein | 4 kcal/g |
| Fat | 9 kcal/g |
| Alcohol | 7 kcal/g |
| Fibre | ~2 kcal/g (variable, from fermentation) |

## Protein

Protein supplies the twenty amino acids used to build enzymes, transporters, antibodies, hormones and structural tissue. Nine are **indispensable (essential)** — histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine — and must come from the diet.

**RDA: 0.8 g per kg body weight per day** for adults, which works out to roughly 46 g/day for a typical adult woman and 56 g/day for a typical adult man. This is a minimum to prevent deficiency in most healthy people, not an optimum. Higher intakes are commonly recommended for older adults (to counter anabolic resistance and sarcopenia), for athletes and for those in a weight-loss deficit; these recommendations come from professional bodies rather than the DRI framework.

Protein quality depends on the amino acid profile and digestibility, assessed by PDCAAS and DIAAS. Animal proteins and soy score highly; most cereals are limited by lysine and most pulses by methionine, which is why combining them across the day works well.

## Carbohydrate

Carbohydrates comprise sugars, starches and fibre. Digestible carbohydrate is the body's most readily available fuel, and glucose is the obligate fuel for red blood cells and, under normal conditions, the preferred fuel of the brain.

**RDA: 130 g/day** for adults — the amount estimated to meet the brain's glucose requirement without relying on ketones or gluconeogenesis. Note that this is a physiological minimum, not a target; the body can adapt to lower intakes, and typical intakes are far higher.

Fibre is carbohydrate that human enzymes cannot digest. The **Adequate Intake is 14 g per 1,000 kcal** — about 25 g/day for adult women and 38 g/day for adult men. Most people fall well short of this.

The quality distinction matters more than the quantity: intact whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruit behave very differently from refined starch and free sugars. The WHO recommends limiting free sugars to under 10% of energy, with a further reduction to under 5% suggested for additional benefit.

## Fat

Fat supplies energy, carries the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, and provides the two essential fatty acids: **linoleic acid** (omega-6) and **alpha-linolenic acid** (omega-3).

Adequate Intakes: linoleic acid 17 g/day (men 19–50) and 12 g/day (women 19–50), falling to 14 g and 11 g respectively after 50; alpha-linolenic acid 1.6 g/day for men and 1.1 g/day for women. Saturated fat is generally capped at under 10% of energy, and industrial trans fat should be as low as possible.

## Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges (AMDR)

The AMDRs define the proportion of total energy from each macronutrient associated with adequate nutrient intake and reduced chronic disease risk in adults:

| Macronutrient | % of total energy |
| :--- | ---: |
| Carbohydrate | 45–65% |
| Fat | 20–35% |
| Protein | 10–35% |

These are deliberately wide. A very large number of eating patterns fall inside them, which is a useful corrective to the idea that one macro split is uniquely correct.

## How to think about it

Macronutrient ratios attract disproportionate attention. In practice, total energy intake, food quality within each macronutrient class, protein adequacy, fibre intake and long-term adherence account for far more of the variance in health outcomes than the precise split between carbohydrate and fat. Individual medical conditions — diabetes, chronic kidney disease, inborn errors of metabolism — change the calculus and warrant individualised advice.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Nutrient Recommendations and Databases](https://ods.od.nih.gov/HealthInformation/nutrientrecommendations.aspx)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [World Health Organization — Healthy diet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/healthy-diet)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/SDA & GLA Sources/oil-omega3-2.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Advanced Plant Omegas: SDA-Rich Oils, GLA Sources, Ahiflower, Echium & Novel Omega-3 Alternatives"
description: "SDA and GLA oils — ahiflower, echium, blackcurrant seed, borage and evening primrose: how they bypass the delta-6 desaturase step, and what the evidence supports."
slug: "oil-omega3-2"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "SDA & GLA Sources"
seoKeywords: ["stearidonic acid", "sda", "gla", "ahiflower", "echium oil", "borage oil", "evening primrose oil", "delta-6 desaturase"]
tags: ["fatty-acid", "omega-3", "omega-6", "plant-oils"]
---

## Overview

Beyond the familiar ALA-rich oils sits a second tier of plant oils containing fatty acids that are one biochemical step further along the elongation-desaturation pathway. The two of interest are **stearidonic acid (SDA, 18:4 n-3)** on the omega-3 side and **gamma-linolenic acid (GLA, 18:3 n-6)** on the omega-6 side.

## Why the extra double bond matters

Conversion of the parent essential fatty acids — ALA to EPA, and linoleic acid to arachidonic acid — is gated by **delta-6 desaturase**, generally the rate-limiting enzyme in both pathways. Its activity is modest in humans and declines with age, alcohol intake, poorly controlled diabetes and deficiencies of the zinc and magnesium cofactors involved.

SDA and GLA are both products of that reaction. Consuming them therefore bypasses the bottleneck. SDA raises tissue EPA substantially more efficiently than an equivalent amount of ALA does — although it still does not raise DHA appreciably, because the later steps to DHA remain limiting. GLA is rapidly elongated to dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA), the precursor of the 1-series prostaglandins, which have anti-inflammatory rather than pro-inflammatory character.

## SDA sources

**Ahiflower oil** (*Buglossoides arvensis*) is the richest commercially available plant source of SDA and also supplies ALA and GLA. **Echium oil** (*Echium plantagineum*) contains SDA, ALA and GLA in a similar mixed profile. **Blackcurrant seed oil** provides SDA alongside GLA. Hemp seed oil contains small amounts of both SDA and GLA.

These oils are marketed as intermediate options for people who do not eat fish and want a more efficient route to EPA than flax provides. That mechanistic claim is reasonably supported; what is not established is that raising EPA by this route produces the clinical outcomes attributed to fish or fish oil. For preformed DHA, algal oil remains the only reliable plant-derived option.

## GLA sources

**Evening primrose oil**, **borage (starflower) oil** — the most GLA-dense of the three — and **blackcurrant seed oil** are the standard GLA supplements. They have been studied for atopic dermatitis, rheumatoid arthritis, cyclical mastalgia and diabetic neuropathy over several decades.

The overall picture is disappointing relative to early enthusiasm. Systematic reviews of evening primrose oil for eczema have not found convincing benefit. Results in rheumatoid arthritis and mastalgia are mixed and largely from small trials. These oils are not harmful in ordinary doses, but they should be described as unproven rather than effective.

**Safety notes:** borage oil from unrefined sources may contain hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids — choose certified PA-free products. GLA oils may interact with anticoagulants and, in some reports, with medications that lower the seizure threshold. Discuss with a clinician before use.

## Practical points

- These are supplement and finishing oils, not cooking oils; all are highly unsaturated and oxidise readily.
- Refrigerate, buy small quantities, and discard if the smell turns sharp or paint-like.
- None of them substitute for the DHA needs of pregnancy, lactation or infancy.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Omega-3 Fatty Acids Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Omega3FattyAcids-HealthProfessional/)
- [NCCIH — Evening Primrose Oil](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/evening-primrose-oil)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Structural Osteo-Minerals/calcium.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Calcium"
description: "Calcium as a structural bone mineral: RDA by age, absorption and vitamin D, dairy and non-dairy food sources, and the 2,500 mg upper limit — per NIH ODS."
slug: "Calcium"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Structural Osteo-Minerals"
seoKeywords: ["calcium", "bone mineral", "hydroxyapatite", "rda", "osteoporosis", "oxalate", "food sources"]
tags: ["essential-mineral", "macromineral", "bone-health"]
---

## Overview

Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body. Roughly 99% of it is locked into the hydroxyapatite crystal lattice of bone and teeth, where it provides structural rigidity; the remaining 1% circulates and is kept within a narrow range because of how critical it is to cell function.

## Why it matters

**Structural role.** Bone is a living tissue in continuous remodelling. Osteoblasts deposit calcium phosphate into a collagen matrix while osteoclasts resorb it. Dietary calcium, together with vitamin D, vitamin K and adequate protein and weight-bearing activity, determines how much mineral is available for that process. Peak bone mass is largely set by the late twenties; after that, adequate intake is about slowing loss rather than building.

**Circulating role.** Ionised calcium drives muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, hormone and neurotransmitter release, and the clotting cascade. Blood calcium is defended by parathyroid hormone, calcitriol and calcitonin — and when dietary intake is chronically low, the body simply withdraws calcium from bone to maintain it. This is why blood calcium is a poor indicator of dietary adequacy.

**Absorption.** Active, vitamin D-dependent transport handles calcium at low intakes; passive paracellular diffusion takes over at higher intakes. Fractional absorption falls as dose rises, which is why splitting supplemental calcium into doses of about 500 mg or less absorbs better than a single large dose. Oxalates (spinach, amaranth) and phytates markedly reduce absorption from those foods.

## Recommended intake

| Group | Amount per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Adults 19–50 | 1,000 mg |
| Women 51+ | 1,200 mg |
| Men 51–70 | 1,000 mg |
| Men 71+ | 1,200 mg |
| Pregnancy/Lactation (19+) | 1,000 mg |

**Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL):** 2,500 mg/day for adults 19–50 and 2,000 mg/day for adults 51+. Excess, usually from supplements, increases the risk of kidney stones and can interfere with iron and zinc absorption.

## Food sources

Milk, yogurt, curd, paneer and cheese; ragi (finger millet); sesame seeds and tahini; almonds; tofu set with calcium sulfate; canned sardines and salmon eaten with the bones; kale, broccoli and bok choy; and fortified plant milks, juices and cereals. Spinach is calcium-rich on paper but its oxalate content makes that calcium poorly available.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Calcium Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Calcium-HealthProfessional/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Sugars, Starches & Fibers/ndb-carb-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Carbohydrate Database: Sugars, Starches, Fiber & the Glycemic Index Reference Table"
description: "A reference guide to carbohydrates: mono- and disaccharides, starch types, resistant starch, fibre, free sugars, and how to interpret glycaemic index and glycaemic load."
slug: "ndb-carb-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Sugars, Starches & Fibers"
seoKeywords: ["carbohydrates", "glycemic index", "glycemic load", "resistant starch", "free sugars", "dietary fibre", "amylose"]
tags: ["carbohydrate", "macronutrient", "reference"]
---

## Overview

Carbohydrates are classified by the number of sugar units they contain and by whether human enzymes can digest them.

**Monosaccharides** — glucose, fructose, galactose.
**Disaccharides** — sucrose (glucose + fructose), lactose (glucose + galactose), maltose (glucose + glucose).
**Oligosaccharides** — 3 to 9 units, including the raffinose-family sugars in pulses and the fructans in wheat, onion and garlic. Largely indigestible and fermented in the colon, which is why they cause gas and why they feature in the FODMAP framework.
**Polysaccharides** — starch (digestible) and the non-starch polysaccharides that make up most dietary fibre.

## Starch

Starch is a glucose polymer in two forms. **Amylose** is linear and packs tightly, digesting more slowly. **Amylopectin** is highly branched, presents more enzyme attack points, and digests rapidly. Rice varieties, potatoes and pulses differ substantially in their amylose-to-amylopectin ratio, which is a large part of why their glycaemic responses differ.

**Resistant starch** escapes digestion in the small intestine and is fermented in the colon, behaving functionally like fibre. Four types are described: physically inaccessible starch in intact grains and seeds (RS1); ungelatinised granular starch in raw potato and green banana (RS2); **retrograded starch** formed when cooked starch is cooled (RS3); and chemically modified starch (RS4). RS3 is the practically interesting one — cooking rice, potatoes or pasta and then cooling them increases resistant starch content, and reheating retains much of it.

## Fibre

Dietary fibre is carbohydrate that human enzymes cannot break down. **Viscous soluble fibres** (beta-glucan, pectin, psyllium, guar) form gels that slow glucose absorption and lower LDL cholesterol by trapping bile acids. **Insoluble fibres** (cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, wheat bran) add stool bulk and speed transit. **Fermentable prebiotic fibres** (inulin, FOS, GOS, resistant starch) feed colonic bacteria and yield short-chain fatty acids.

**Adequate Intake: 14 g per 1,000 kcal** — approximately 25 g/day for adult women and 38 g/day for adult men.

## Free sugars

"Free sugars" means sugars added to foods plus those naturally present in honey, syrups and fruit juice. Sugars intrinsic to whole fruit, vegetables and milk are excluded, because the food matrix changes how they behave. The WHO recommends limiting free sugars to **under 10% of total energy**, with a conditional further recommendation to go below 5%.

## Glycaemic index and glycaemic load

**Glycaemic index (GI)** ranks a food by the blood glucose response to a 50 g available-carbohydrate portion, relative to pure glucose (GI 100). Conventionally: low ≤55, medium 56–69, high ≥70.

**Glycaemic load (GL)** multiplies GI by the grams of available carbohydrate in a realistic serving and divides by 100. It corrects the main weakness of GI. Watermelon is the standard illustration — high GI, but so little carbohydrate per serving that its glycaemic load is low. Conventionally: low ≤10, medium 11–19, high ≥20.

**How to use these numbers carefully.** GI is measured on foods eaten alone, in fasted subjects, and published values carry wide confidence intervals. In real meals the response is modified by fat, protein, acidity (vinegar, curd, lemon), fibre, particle size, degree of processing, ripeness, cooking time and cooling, and by considerable person-to-person variation. GI is a useful comparative concept within a food category — parboiled versus polished rice, intact versus rolled oats, pasta cooked al dente versus soft — and a poor tool for ranking whole diets. It is not a proxy for healthfulness: fructose and full-fat ice cream have low GI values.

## Recommended intake

The RDA for carbohydrate is 130 g/day for adults, based on the brain's glucose requirement. The Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range is 45–65% of energy. Both are population reference values; individual needs vary with activity, body size and medical conditions.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [World Health Organization — Guideline: Sugars intake for adults and children](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Nutrient Recommendations and Databases](https://ods.od.nih.gov/HealthInformation/nutrientrecommendations.aspx)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; people with diabetes should discuss carbohydrate management with their clinician.*
