FILE: Nutrient Database/Sulfur/min-s-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Sulfur: Cysteine, Methionine, MSM, Glutathione & the Structural Mineral in Proteins & Detoxification"
description: "Dietary sulfur: methionine and cysteine, disulfide bonds, glutathione and sulfation pathways, food sources, and an honest look at MSM supplements."
slug: "min-s-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Sulfur"
seoKeywords: ["sulfur", "methionine", "cysteine", "glutathione", "msm", "sulfation", "transsulfuration", "food sources"]
tags: ["mineral", "amino-acid", "detoxification"]
---

## Overview

Sulfur is abundant in the body but is not handled like other minerals. There is no dietary reference intake for elemental sulfur, because humans obtain essentially all of it as part of the sulfur-containing amino acids **methionine** (essential) and **cysteine** (conditionally essential), plus small contributions from thiamine, biotin and inorganic sulfate in food and water.

## Why it matters

**Protein structure.** Cysteine residues form disulfide bridges that lock proteins into their functional three-dimensional shape. Keratin in hair, skin and nails is exceptionally cysteine-rich, which is why burning hair smells of sulfur and why severe protein deficiency shows up first in these tissues.

**Glutathione.** The tripeptide glutathione (glutamate-cysteine-glycine) is the cell's principal intracellular antioxidant and a substrate for glutathione peroxidase and glutathione S-transferase. Cysteine availability is generally the rate-limiting step in its synthesis. Glutathione conjugation is a major phase II pathway for clearing electrophilic compounds — including the pathway that becomes overwhelmed in paracetamol overdose, which is treated with N-acetylcysteine precisely to restore cysteine supply.

**Sulfation.** Sulfate groups derived from cysteine metabolism are transferred onto steroid hormones, neurotransmitters, bile acids and drugs to make them water-soluble for excretion. Sulfated glycosaminoglycans such as chondroitin sulfate are structural components of cartilage and connective tissue.

**One-carbon metabolism.** Methionine is the precursor of S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe), the universal methyl donor. After donating its methyl group it becomes homocysteine, which is either remethylated (using folate and B12) or committed to cysteine synthesis through the transsulfuration pathway, which requires vitamin B6. Sulfur amino acid metabolism is therefore inseparable from B-vitamin status.

## Food sources

Methionine and cysteine are concentrated in animal protein — eggs (egg white is particularly rich), fish, poultry, meat and dairy. Plant sources include soy, legumes (generally lower in methionine), sesame and sunflower seeds, Brazil nuts, and oats. Allium vegetables (garlic, onion, leek) and cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, mustard greens, radish) contribute distinctive organosulfur compounds — allicin, sulforaphane and glucosinolates — that are the subject of considerable research interest, though most of that work is preclinical or observational.

A varied diet meeting protein requirements supplies adequate sulfur amino acids. Dedicated sulfur deficiency is not a recognised clinical entity separate from protein deficiency.

## A note on MSM and sulfur supplements

Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM) is widely marketed for joint pain and inflammation. It is generally well tolerated in the doses studied, but the human trial evidence is limited in size and quality and does not support strong claims. The same applies to "sulfur nourish" protocols — sulfation and glutathione conjugation are genuine biochemical pathways, but the idea that they need supplemental boosting in a well-nourished person is not established. Anyone considering these products should discuss them with a clinician, particularly alongside other medication.

## Sources

- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Dietary Supplement Fact Sheets](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Systemic Electrolytes/potassium-chloride.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Potassium Chloride"
description: "Potassium chloride: potassium's role in blood pressure and cell function, the adult AI, food sources, salt substitutes and why supplements need caution — per NIH ODS."
slug: "Potassium Chloride"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Systemic Electrolytes"
seoKeywords: ["potassium chloride", "potassium", "adequate intake", "blood pressure", "salt substitute", "hyperkalaemia"]
tags: ["essential-mineral", "electrolyte", "macromineral"]
---

## Overview

Potassium chloride (KCl) is the potassium salt used in supplements, in intravenous replacement, and as the main ingredient in low-sodium "salt substitutes". Potassium itself is the principal intracellular cation, and its balance with extracellular sodium underpins almost every excitable process in the body.

## Why potassium matters

The sodium-potassium ATPase pump maintains a steep gradient — potassium high inside cells, sodium high outside — and the resulting membrane potential is what allows nerves to fire and muscle, including cardiac muscle, to contract. Potassium also participates in fluid balance, acid-base regulation and glucose and glycogen handling.

**Blood pressure.** Higher dietary potassium is associated with lower blood pressure and lower stroke risk, in part because potassium promotes urinary sodium excretion and relaxes vascular smooth muscle. Most populations consume far less potassium and far more sodium than recommended, and shifting that ratio toward more unprocessed plant foods is one of the better-supported dietary levers for cardiovascular health.

**Deficiency (hypokalaemia)** is usually caused by losses rather than low intake: vomiting, diarrhoea, laxative misuse, thiazide and loop diuretics. It causes weakness, cramps, constipation and, when severe, arrhythmias.

**Excess (hyperkalaemia)** is the mirror risk and can be fatal. It arises with reduced kidney function and with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and potassium-sparing diuretics. Because of this, over-the-counter potassium supplements are limited in dose in many markets, and **salt substitutes containing potassium chloride are not safe for everyone** — people with chronic kidney disease or on those medications should use them only on medical advice.

## Recommended intake

There is no RDA for potassium; an Adequate Intake is set.

| Group | Amount per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Men 19+ | 3,400 mg |
| Women 19+ | 2,600 mg |
| Pregnancy (19+) | 2,900 mg |
| Lactation (19+) | 2,800 mg |

No Tolerable Upper Intake Level has been set for healthy people with normal kidney function.

## Food sources

Potatoes and sweet potatoes with skin, beans and lentils, bananas, coconut water, tomatoes and tomato paste, spinach and other greens, avocado, oranges, dried apricots, curd and milk, and fish such as salmon. Whole, minimally processed foods are the reliable route to adequate potassium.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Potassium Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Potassium-HealthProfessional/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Systemic Electrolytes/sodium-chloride.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Sodium Chloride"
description: "Sodium chloride (salt): sodium's physiological role, the 1,500 mg AI and 2,300 mg reduction target, where dietary salt actually comes from, and practical reduction."
slug: "Sodium Chloride - Database"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Systemic Electrolytes"
seoKeywords: ["sodium chloride", "salt", "sodium intake", "blood pressure", "chronic disease risk reduction", "hyponatraemia"]
tags: ["essential-mineral", "electrolyte", "macromineral"]
---

## Overview

Sodium chloride is common salt. By weight it is roughly 40% sodium and 60% chloride, so 1 gram of salt supplies about 400 mg of sodium — a conversion worth remembering, because dietary guidance is written in sodium while food labels and recipes are often written in salt.

## Why it matters

Sodium is the main extracellular cation and the principal determinant of extracellular fluid volume. Together with potassium it sets the membrane potential that drives nerve conduction and muscle contraction, and it powers the co-transporters that absorb glucose and amino acids in the gut and reabsorb them in the kidney. Chloride is not a passive partner: it is essential for gastric hydrochloric acid, for the chloride shift that transports carbon dioxide in blood, and for acid-base balance.

The physiological requirement for sodium is small. Almost everyone consumes far more than needed, and the relationship between habitual sodium intake, blood pressure, and risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease is one of the most consistently reported in nutrition epidemiology.

**Too little** is generally a clinical rather than a dietary problem. Hyponatraemia arises from excess water intake relative to sodium, SIADH, diuretics, heart or liver failure — and occasionally in endurance athletes who drink large volumes of plain water. It causes headache, confusion, seizures and, if severe, cerebral oedema.

## Recommended intake

| Reference value (adults 19+) | Sodium per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Adequate Intake (AI) | 1,500 mg |
| Chronic Disease Risk Reduction (CDRR) intake | reduce intake if above 2,300 mg |

The CDRR is not an upper limit in the classical toxicological sense — it is the level above which reducing intake is expected to lower chronic disease risk. Most national guidelines set a practical target at or below 2,000–2,300 mg sodium (about 5–6 g of salt) per day.

## Where dietary sodium actually comes from

In most diets the salt shaker is a minority contributor. The bulk comes from processed and packaged foods: bread and bakery products, biscuits and namkeen, papad and pickles, managed and processed meats, cheese, instant noodles, soups and stock cubes, sauces and condiments including soy sauce and ketchup, and restaurant food. Reducing sodium meaningfully therefore means changing what is bought, not just what is added at the table.

Practical steps: read labels and compare per 100 g; use herbs, spices, citrus, tamarind and vinegar to carry flavour; drain and rinse canned pulses; and reduce salt gradually, since taste preference adapts over a few weeks. Potassium-based salt substitutes help some people but are unsuitable in kidney disease or on potassium-retaining medication.

## Sources

- [NASEM — Dietary Reference Intakes for Sodium and Potassium (2019)](https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/25353/dietary-reference-intakes-for-sodium-and-potassium)
- [U.S. FDA — Sodium in Your Diet](https://www.fda.gov/food/nutrition-education-resources-materials/sodium-your-diet)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss dietary changes with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Vitamin A/vit-a-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Vitamin A: Retinol, Beta-Carotene, RAE & the Vision, Immunity & Skin Vitamin"
description: "Vitamin A explained: preformed retinol vs provitamin A carotenoids, retinol activity equivalents, RDA, deficiency and xerophthalmia, food sources and the 3,000 mcg UL."
slug: "vit-a-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Vitamin A"
seoKeywords: ["vitamin a", "retinol", "beta-carotene", "rae", "xerophthalmia", "night blindness", "rda", "upper limit"]
tags: ["vitamin", "fat-soluble", "micronutrient"]
---

## Overview

Vitamin A is not one compound but a family. **Preformed vitamin A** (retinol and retinyl esters) comes from animal foods and is directly usable. **Provitamin A carotenoids** — chiefly beta-carotene, with alpha-carotene and beta-cryptoxanthin — come from plants and must be cleaved and converted. Lycopene, lutein and zeaxanthin are carotenoids with no vitamin A activity.

## Function

**Vision.** Retinal binds to opsin in the rod cells of the retina to form rhodopsin, the pigment responsible for vision in low light. Impaired regeneration of rhodopsin is why night blindness is the earliest symptom of deficiency.

**Gene regulation and epithelia.** Retinoic acid binds nuclear retinoic acid and retinoid X receptors and regulates transcription of genes controlling cell differentiation. This keeps epithelial surfaces — cornea and conjunctiva, respiratory tract, gut and skin — properly differentiated and mucus-secreting.

**Immunity.** Vitamin A supports both barrier integrity and adaptive immune function; deficiency substantially increases mortality from measles and diarrhoeal disease in children, which is the basis of WHO supplementation programmes.

**Growth and reproduction.** Retinoic acid signalling is essential in embryonic development, spermatogenesis and bone remodelling.

## Recommended intake

Intakes are expressed as **retinol activity equivalents (RAE)**: 1 mcg RAE = 1 mcg retinol = 12 mcg dietary beta-carotene = 24 mcg dietary alpha-carotene or beta-cryptoxanthin.

| Group | Amount per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Men 19+ | 900 mcg RAE |
| Women 19+ | 700 mcg RAE |
| Pregnancy (19+) | 770 mcg RAE |
| Lactation (19+) | 1,300 mcg RAE |

**Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL):** 3,000 mcg/day of **preformed** vitamin A for adults. The UL does not apply to provitamin A carotenoids, whose conversion is regulated.

## Deficiency

Vitamin A deficiency remains a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness. It progresses from night blindness through conjunctival dryness and Bitot's spots to corneal xerosis, ulceration and keratomalacia (collectively xerophthalmia). It also causes follicular hyperkeratosis of the skin, impaired growth and increased infectious mortality. Risk is highest in young children, pregnant women in low-income settings, and people with fat malabsorption — cystic fibrosis, coeliac disease, cholestatic liver disease or after bariatric surgery.

## Too much

Acute hypervitaminosis A causes headache, nausea, blurred vision and raised intracranial pressure. Chronic excess causes liver injury, bone loss and fracture, dry skin, hair loss and joint pain. Critically, **high-dose preformed vitamin A is teratogenic** — pregnant women should avoid liver, high-dose supplements and oral retinoid medications such as isotretinoin. Beta-carotene from food does not cause toxicity, though very high intakes turn the skin orange (harmless carotenaemia). High-dose beta-carotene *supplements* increased lung cancer incidence among smokers in large trials and should be avoided by that group.

## Food sources

Preformed: liver (extremely concentrated), cod liver oil, egg yolk, butter, ghee, whole milk and cheese, and fortified foods.
Provitamin A: carrot, sweet potato, pumpkin, red and orange capsicum, mango, papaya, apricot, and dark leafy greens such as spinach, amaranth, methi and drumstick leaves. Cooking, chopping and eating with a little fat all improve carotenoid absorption.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin A and Carotenoids Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminA-HealthProfessional/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Vitamin D/vit-d-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Vitamin D: D2 vs. D3, 25(OH)D Testing & the Sunshine Hormone for Bones, Immunity & Mood"
description: "Vitamin D explained: skin synthesis, D2 vs D3, what a 25(OH)D test means, RDA, food sources, who is at risk of deficiency, and the 4,000 IU upper limit."
slug: "vit-d-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Vitamin D"
seoKeywords: ["vitamin d", "25-hydroxyvitamin d", "cholecalciferol", "ergocalciferol", "rickets", "deficiency", "rda", "sunlight"]
tags: ["vitamin", "fat-soluble", "micronutrient"]
---

## Overview

Vitamin D is unusual among vitamins in that the body can make it. UVB radiation converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin to cholecalciferol (D3). It is also unusual in acting as a **hormone** rather than a coenzyme.

Two dietary forms exist: **D3 (cholecalciferol)** from animal foods, lanolin and most supplements, and **D2 (ergocalciferol)** from UV-exposed fungi and yeast. Both raise blood levels; D3 is generally somewhat more effective at sustaining them, especially with intermittent dosing.

## How it works

Vitamin D from skin or diet is hydroxylated in the liver to **25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol)** — the storage and transport form, and the one measured in blood tests. The kidney then converts it to **1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol)**, the active hormone, under tight control by parathyroid hormone, phosphate and FGF23.

Calcitriol binds the vitamin D receptor, present in intestine, bone, kidney, parathyroid and many immune cells. Its principal job is to raise intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption so that bone can mineralise. Without it, calcium absorption falls sharply, PTH rises, and bone mineral is withdrawn to defend blood calcium.

## Interpreting a 25(OH)D test

Laboratories report 25(OH)D in nmol/L or ng/mL (divide nmol/L by 2.5 for ng/mL). The Institute of Medicine considers levels below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) as deficient and puts sufficiency for bone health at 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) or above; some clinical societies set a higher target. There is genuine disagreement here, and routine screening of asymptomatic people is not recommended by most guidelines. Testing makes sense when there is clinical reason — bone disease, malabsorption, unexplained symptoms, or a high-risk profile.

## Recommended intake

| Group | Amount per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Adults 19–70 | 15 mcg (600 IU) |
| Adults 71+ | 20 mcg (800 IU) |
| Pregnancy/Lactation | 15 mcg (600 IU) |

**Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL):** 100 mcg (4,000 IU)/day for adults.

## Deficiency

Deficiency causes **rickets** in children — bowed legs, widened growth plates, delayed fontanelle closure — and **osteomalacia** in adults, with bone pain and proximal muscle weakness. Lesser degrees contribute to secondary hyperparathyroidism and bone loss.

Risk factors: limited sun exposure (indoor work, extensive clothing cover, long winters at high latitude), darker skin pigmentation (melanin competes for UVB), older age (reduced skin synthesis), obesity (sequestration in adipose tissue), exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation, fat malabsorption, and chronic kidney or liver disease. Deficiency is common even in sunny countries, largely because of sun avoidance and clothing coverage.

## On immunity, mood and other claims

Vitamin D receptors are widespread, and low 25(OH)D is associated with many conditions in observational studies. Randomised trials, however, have largely failed to show that supplementing people who are not deficient prevents cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or depression. Some meta-analyses suggest a modest reduction in acute respiratory infection, mainly in those who were deficient to begin with. The reasonable position: correcting genuine deficiency is worthwhile and well-supported; high-dose supplementation of already-replete people is not.

## Too much

Toxicity comes from supplements, never from sunlight. It causes hypercalcaemia — nausea, vomiting, weakness, frequent urination, confusion — and can lead to kidney stones, renal impairment and vascular calcification. Very high intermittent bolus doses have, in some trials, been associated with increased falls in older adults.

## Food sources

Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring), cod liver oil, egg yolk, liver, UV-exposed mushrooms (D2), and fortified milk, plant milks, cereals and spreads. Few unfortified foods contribute much, which is why sun exposure and, where appropriate, supplementation matter.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin D Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminD-HealthProfessional/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Vitamin E/vit-e-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Vitamin E: Alpha-Tocopherol, Gamma-Tocopherol, Tocotrienols & the Lipid-Soluble Antioxidant"
description: "Vitamin E explained: the eight vitamers, why only alpha-tocopherol counts toward requirements, natural vs synthetic forms, RDA, food sources and the 1,000 mg UL."
slug: "vit-e-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Vitamin E"
seoKeywords: ["vitamin e", "alpha-tocopherol", "gamma-tocopherol", "tocotrienols", "rda", "antioxidant", "upper limit"]
tags: ["vitamin", "fat-soluble", "antioxidant"]
---

## Overview

Vitamin E is a family of eight fat-soluble compounds: four **tocopherols** (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) and four **tocotrienols** with the same designations. They differ in the methylation of the chromanol ring and in whether the side chain is saturated (tocopherols) or unsaturated (tocotrienols).

Only **alpha-tocopherol** meets the human requirement. The liver's alpha-tocopherol transfer protein selectively loads it onto VLDL for distribution; the other vitamers are largely metabolised and excreted. Dietary reference intakes therefore refer to alpha-tocopherol alone.

## Function

Alpha-tocopherol is the principal chain-breaking antioxidant of cell membranes and lipoproteins. Polyunsaturated fatty acids in membranes are vulnerable to attack by lipid peroxyl radicals, which propagate a self-sustaining chain reaction. Alpha-tocopherol donates a hydrogen atom to terminate that chain, becoming a relatively stable tocopheroxyl radical which vitamin C and other reductants regenerate. It also has non-antioxidant roles: inhibition of protein kinase C, modulation of gene expression, and inhibition of platelet aggregation — the last explaining the bleeding risk at high doses.

**Gamma-tocopherol** deserves a mention: it is the dominant form in many vegetable oils and in the typical diet, and unlike alpha-tocopherol it can trap reactive nitrogen species. It is nonetheless preferentially excreted, and high-dose alpha-tocopherol supplements lower plasma gamma-tocopherol — one reason isolated high-dose supplementation is viewed cautiously.

**Tocotrienols**, concentrated in palm, rice bran and annatto, are an active research area for lipid and neuroprotective effects, but human evidence is preliminary and they do not count toward vitamin E requirements.

## Natural vs synthetic

Natural vitamin E is **RRR-alpha-tocopherol**, labelled *d*-alpha-tocopherol. Synthetic vitamin E is **all-*rac*-alpha-tocopherol** (*dl*-alpha), an equal mix of eight stereoisomers of which only some are retained by the transfer protein. Natural-source vitamin E therefore has higher biological activity per milligram, and the old IU conversions differ between the two forms.

## Recommended intake

| Group | Amount per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Adults 19+ | 15 mg |
| Pregnancy | 15 mg |
| Lactation | 19 mg |

**Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL):** 1,000 mg/day of supplemental alpha-tocopherol for adults, set on the basis of haemorrhagic risk.

## Deficiency

Dietary deficiency is rare. It occurs almost exclusively in fat-malabsorption states — cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease, short bowel syndrome — and in the rare genetic disorders abetalipoproteinaemia and ataxia with isolated vitamin E deficiency. Features are neurological: peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, loss of proprioception, myopathy and retinopathy, along with red-cell fragility.

## Too much

High-dose supplements can impair platelet aggregation and potentiate warfarin and antiplatelet drugs, raising bleeding risk. Meta-analyses of high-dose vitamin E supplement trials have not shown benefit for cardiovascular disease or cancer prevention, and some have raised concern about all-cause mortality at high doses. Vitamin E from food carries no such concerns.

## Food sources

Wheat germ oil, sunflower seeds and sunflower oil, safflower oil, almonds, hazelnuts, peanuts and peanut butter, avocado, mango, spinach, broccoli and other green leafy vegetables, and red capsicum.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin E Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminE-HealthProfessional/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*


========================================================================
FILE: Nutrient Database/Vitamin K/vit-k-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Vitamin K: K1 Phylloquinone, K2 MK-4 & MK-7, Osteocalcin & the Calcium-Directing Vitamin"
description: "Vitamin K explained: K1 vs K2, gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors and Gla proteins, adequate intakes, warfarin interaction, newborn prophylaxis and food sources."
slug: "vit-k-1"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-25
subCategory: "Vitamin K"
seoKeywords: ["vitamin k", "phylloquinone", "menaquinone", "mk-7", "osteocalcin", "warfarin", "adequate intake", "clotting"]
tags: ["vitamin", "fat-soluble", "micronutrient"]
---

## Overview

Vitamin K is a group of fat-soluble compounds sharing a naphthoquinone ring. **Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone)** is made by plants and dominates the diet. **Vitamin K2 (menaquinones, MK-n)** is produced by bacteria and found in fermented foods and animal tissues; MK-4 and MK-7 are the forms of practical interest. Synthetic menadione (K3) is not used in human supplements.

## Function

Vitamin K is the cofactor for **gamma-glutamyl carboxylase**, which converts specific glutamate residues in target proteins to gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla). Only after this modification can these proteins bind calcium and function. In the process vitamin K is oxidised, then recycled by vitamin K epoxide reductase — the enzyme warfarin inhibits.

**Coagulation.** Clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X, and the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z, all require carboxylation. Deficiency prolongs prothrombin time and causes bleeding.

**Bone.** Osteocalcin, secreted by osteoblasts, is a vitamin K-dependent protein involved in binding calcium to the bone matrix. Undercarboxylated osteocalcin is a sensitive marker of vitamin K status and has been associated with lower bone density in observational studies.

**Vascular tissue.** Matrix Gla protein, made in vascular smooth muscle and cartilage, is a powerful inhibitor of soft-tissue calcification. This is the "calcium-directing" idea behind vitamin K — keeping calcium in bone and out of arteries. It is biologically well-founded, but the intervention evidence that supplementation improves fracture or cardiovascular outcomes in well-nourished people is not yet convincing. Treat it as promising, not proven.

## K1 vs K2 in practice

Phylloquinone is cleared rapidly by the liver and mainly supports coagulation. MK-7, with its long isoprenoid side chain, has a much longer circulating half-life and reaches bone and vessel wall more effectively — the pharmacokinetic basis for interest in K2 supplements. Gut bacteria also synthesise menaquinones, though the contribution of colonic synthesis to human status is uncertain.

## Recommended intake

No RDA has been set; Adequate Intakes are used, and they apply to total vitamin K.

| Group | Amount per day |
| :--- | ---: |
| Men 19+ | 120 mcg |
| Women 19+ | 90 mcg |
| Pregnancy/Lactation (19+) | 90 mcg |

No Tolerable Upper Intake Level has been established.

## Deficiency

Dietary deficiency in healthy adults is rare. It occurs with fat malabsorption, cholestatic liver disease, prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics, and in **newborns**, who are born with low stores, receive little in breast milk and have a sterile gut. Vitamin K prophylaxis at birth prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding and is standard practice worldwide.

## The warfarin interaction

Vitamin K antagonists work by blocking vitamin K recycling, so vitamin K intake directly opposes them. The correct advice is **consistency, not avoidance** — patients on warfarin should keep their intake of green vegetables steady rather than eliminating them, and should discuss any vitamin K supplement, including K2, with the prescribing clinician. Direct oral anticoagulants do not have this interaction.

## Food sources

**K1:** kale, spinach, collard, mustard and turnip greens, coriander and parsley leaf, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, lettuce, and soybean and canola oil.
**K2:** natto (by far the richest MK-7 source), hard and soft cheeses, curd, egg yolk, butter, liver and dark chicken meat.

Absorption improves when these foods are eaten with some fat.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamin K Health Professional Fact Sheet](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminK-HealthProfessional/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-25. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss supplementation with a qualified clinician.*

FILE: Nutrient Database/nutrient-database.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Nutrient Database"
description: "A reference guide to essential nutrients, the Dietary Reference Intake framework (EAR, RDA, AI, UL), and how to read food composition data from USDA FoodData Central."
slug: "nutrient-database"
category: "Nutrient Database"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "NutritionColours Medical Review Board"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-30
subCategory: "Nutrient Database"
seoKeywords: ["nutrient database", "dietary reference intakes", "rda", "tolerable upper intake level", "food composition data", "usda fooddata central", "essential nutrients"]
tags: ["reference", "nutrient-data"]
---

## Overview

This section is the reference layer of the site: what each nutrient does, how much of it people need, which foods supply it, and where the numbers come from. This page explains the framework the rest of the section uses.

An **essential nutrient** is one the body cannot make at all, or cannot make in sufficient quantity, and must therefore obtain from food. Essential nutrients fall into two broad groups:

- **Macronutrients**, needed in gram quantities and supplying energy: carbohydrate, protein (specifically the nine indispensable amino acids), and fat (including the essential fatty acids linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid). Water is also required in large amounts, though it supplies no energy. Dietary fibre is not strictly essential but has well-established health effects.
- **Micronutrients**, needed in milligram or microgram quantities: 13 vitamins — A, C, D, E, K, thiamin (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pantothenic acid (B5), vitamin B6, biotin (B7), folate (B9), and vitamin B12 — plus the essential minerals, conventionally split into major minerals (calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chloride, sulphur) and trace elements (iron, zinc, copper, manganese, iodine, selenium, molybdenum, chromium, fluoride).

## How intake recommendations work

Most of the reference values used on this site come from the **Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs)**, developed by expert committees convened by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine and summarised by the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements. Four values do most of the work, and they are frequently confused:

| Term | What it means | How to use it |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **EAR** (Estimated Average Requirement) | The intake estimated to meet the needs of half the healthy people in a group | Used to assess and plan intakes for populations, not individuals |
| **RDA** (Recommended Dietary Allowance) | The intake estimated to meet the needs of nearly all (97–98%) healthy people in a group | The usual individual goal, where one exists |
| **AI** (Adequate Intake) | An observed or estimated intake assumed to be adequate, set when data are insufficient for an RDA | Used as a goal in place of an RDA |
| **UL** (Tolerable Upper Intake Level) | The highest chronic daily intake unlikely to cause adverse effects | A ceiling, not a target |

Three points are worth emphasising. Values are **age- and sex-specific**, with separate figures for pregnancy and lactation — a single number for "adults" is almost always an oversimplification. An RDA is a **goal for habitual intake**, not a daily quota to hit exactly; averaged over a week is fine. And a UL usually refers to **total intake from supplements, fortified foods, and in some cases food combined** — the definition varies by nutrient and is stated on each fact sheet.

Separately, food labels in the United States use the **Daily Value (DV)**, a single reference figure per nutrient chosen for labelling simplicity. DVs are derived from the DRIs but are not the same thing, and the percentages on a label will not always match the RDA for your age group.

## Reading food composition data

Nutrient content figures on this site are drawn from **USDA FoodData Central**, which combines several distinct data types that should not be treated as interchangeable:

- **Foundation Foods** — recent analytical values for single foods, with information on sampling and variability.
- **SR Legacy** — the historical Standard Reference dataset; broad coverage, but some entries are old.
- **FNDDS** (Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies) — values for foods and mixed dishes as consumed, used for national dietary surveys.
- **Branded Foods** — label data supplied by manufacturers, which reflects declared rather than analysed values.

Composition data has real limits. Nutrient content varies with cultivar, soil, season, ripeness, storage, and preparation; selenium and iodine in plant foods depend heavily on where they were grown. Cooking changes both content and weight, so a "per 100 g" figure for raw and cooked versions of the same food is not comparable. Water-soluble vitamins, especially vitamin C, thiamin, and folate, are lost to heat and to cooking water. And **content is not the same as bioavailability** — how much is actually absorbed and used depends on the chemical form, the rest of the meal, and the individual's status, which is covered in the *Absorption, Enhancers & Inhibitors* subsection.

## Using this section

Each nutrient page follows the same structure: what the nutrient does, how much is recommended, which foods supply it, what deficiency looks like, and what happens with too much. Where a figure would be misleading without context, we describe the requirement qualitatively and link to the primary source rather than reproducing a number out of context.

Nutrient requirements shown here apply to generally healthy people. Pregnancy, lactation, infancy, chronic kidney or liver disease, malabsorption conditions, bariatric surgery, and many medications all change requirements — sometimes substantially, and sometimes downwards. Use these pages to understand the landscape, and a clinician or registered dietitian to set your own targets.

## Sources

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Nutrient Recommendations and Databases](https://ods.od.nih.gov/HealthInformation/nutrientrecommendations.aspx)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Dietary Supplement Fact Sheets (all nutrients)](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/)
- [USDA FoodData Central](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/)
- [National Academies — Dietary Reference Intakes](https://www.nationalacademies.org/our-work/summary-report-of-the-dietary-reference-intakes)

*Clinically reviewed by the NutritionColours Medical Review Board. Last reviewed 2026-07-30. Educational information, not medical advice; discuss individual nutrient targets and supplementation with a qualified clinician.*

FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Accessory Fruits/berry-acc-1.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Apple: Red Delicious, Granny Smith, Honeycrisp, Fuji & 7,500+ Varieties"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Apple: Red Delicious, Granny Smith, Honeycrisp, Fuji & 7,500+ Varieties."
slug: "berry-acc-1"
category: "Fruits"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
subCategory: "Accessory Fruits"
seoKeywords: ["berry-acc-1", "accessory fruits", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Apples (*Malus domestica*) are globally cultivated accessory pome fruits belonging to the Rosaceae family. Encompassing over 7,500 varieties including Red Delicious, Granny Smith, Honeycrisp, and Fuji, apples supply high concentrations of soluble pectin fiber, vitamin C, and bioavailable polyphenols. Regular dietary inclusion promotes cardiovascular protection, glycemic management, and microflora diversity.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

A medium apple (approx. 182g) provides roughly 95 calories, 4.4 grams of dietary fiber, and 14% of the Daily Value for vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid). It delivers trace amounts of potassium, copper, manganese, and vitamin K. Pectin, the predominant soluble fiber in apples, forms a viscous gel matrix in the digestive canal. This retards gastric emptying, moderates glucose absorption rate, and contributes to a favorable glycemic index of 36.

Apples possess a rich phenolic spectrum, primarily concentrated within the pericarp (peel). Key flavonoids include quercetin (specifically quercetin-3-rutinoside and quercetin-3-galactoside), catechin, epicatechin, phloridzin, and cyanidin-3-galactoside in red-skinned cultivars. Quercetin exhibits potent antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties by scavenging free radicals and downregulating NF-κB signaling. Phloridzin, a dihydrochalcone unique to apples, inhibits renal sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2), offering potential benefits for blood glucose regulation.

Epidemiological studies demonstrate that routine apple consumption is associated with a reduced incidence of ischemic stroke, hypercholesterolemia, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Fermentation of apple pectin by colonic microbes produces short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, and butyrate), which lower colonic pH, nourish colonocytes, and suppress pathogenic bacteria growth.

## Practical notes

- **Selection**: Choose apples that are firm, heavy for their size, with clean, unblemished skin and intact stems. Tart, dense varieties (Granny Smith, Braeburn) suit cooking, while crisp, sweet-tart cultivars (Honeycrisp, Fuji, Gala) are preferred for fresh consumption.
- **Storage**: Refrigerate apples in the crisper drawer at 30–35°F (-1–2°C) with high humidity. Apples release ethylene gas, which accelerates ripening in nearby produce, so store them separately or in perforated plastic bags. Properly refrigerated apples maintain quality for several weeks.
- **Preparation**: Wash thoroughly under cold running water before eating to remove surface wax and residues. Consume skin-on whenever possible to maximize polyphenol and fiber intake. To prevent enzyme-driven browning (polyphenol oxidase) on cut slices, toss with dilute lemon juice or cold saltwater.

## Safety note

Apple seeds contain amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside that hydrolyzes into hydrogen cyanide upon enzymatic cleavage when chewed or crushed. While accidental swallowing of intact seeds poses negligible risk due to the tough seed coat, intentional crushing and mass consumption of seeds must be avoided. Individuals with oral allergy syndrome (OAS) associated with birch pollen allergy may experience mild localized itching of the lips and mouth when eating raw apples due to protein cross-reactivity (Bet v 1 homolog Bet v 1/Mal d 1).

## Sources

- USDA FoodData Central. *Apples, raw, with skin (NDB Number: 09003)*. U.S. Department of Agriculture.
- National Institutes of Health (NIH). *Flavonoids and Cardiovascular Health: Role of Apples and Quercetin*. PubMed Central.
- Hyson, D. A. (2011). A Comprehensive Review of Apples and Apple Components and Their Relationship to Human Health. *Advances in Nutrition*, 2(5), 408–420.

FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Accessory Fruits/berry-acc-2.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Pear: Bartlett, Bosc, Anjou, Asian & Comice — Grit Cells, Ripening & Poire"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Pear: Bartlett, Bosc, Anjou, Asian & Comice — Grit Cells, Ripening & Poire."
slug: "berry-acc-2"
category: "Fruits"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
subCategory: "Accessory Fruits"
seoKeywords: ["berry-acc-2", "accessory fruits", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Pears (*Pyrus communis* and *Pyrus pyrifolia*) are accessory pome fruits characterized by edible receptacle tissue surrounding a central core. Cultivars like Bartlett, Bosc, Anjou, Comice, and Asian pear offer diverse textures shaped by stone cells or sclereids. Rich in dietary fiber, polyphenols, and micronutrients, pears support cardiovascular, metabolic, and digestive health.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Pears are an excellent source of essential dietary fiber, particularly pectin, providing approximately 6 grams per medium fruit (21% Daily Value). They contain significant quantities of vitamin C (ascorbic acid), vitamin K (phylloquinone), copper, and potassium. Copper acts as a vital cofactor for superoxide dismutase and cytochrome c oxidase, while potassium assists in osmotic homeostasis and vascular tone regulation. Pears also exhibit a low glycemic index (~38), preventing rapid postprandial glucose spikes.

The phytochemical profile of pears is rich in phenolic acids, arbutin, and flavonoids such as quercetin, epicatechin, and chlorogenic acid, concentrated predominantly in the skin. Arbutin exerts mild antimicrobial activity, while chlorogenic acid reduces systemic oxidative stress and improves insulin sensitivity. The granular texture characteristic of European pears stems from sclereids (grit cells)—lignified cell walls containing cellulose and lignin that act as insoluble bulking agents in the gastrointestinal tract.

Clinical studies indicate that regular consumption of pears contributes to lower risks of type 2 diabetes, stroke, and coronary heart disease. Soluble pectin binds bile acids in the intestinal lumen, promoting cholesterol excretion and supporting short-chain fatty acid synthesis by gut microbiota. Furthermore, the high water content and balanced fructose-to-glucose ratio enhance stool transit and colonic health.

## Practical notes

- **Selection**: Choose pears that are firm to the touch with undamaged skin. For European varieties (Bartlett, Bosc, Anjou, Comice), test for ripeness by pressing gently near the stem ("check the neck"); yield to gentle pressure indicates readiness. Asian pears should be selected firm and aromatic.
- **Storage**: Store unripe pears at room temperature to allow interior ripening, as pears mature from the inside out. Once ripened to desired softness, transfer to the refrigerator (32–35°F / 0–2°C) for up to 3–5 days to slow degradation.
- **Preparation**: Wash thoroughly under cool running water. Retain the nutrient-dense peel whenever possible. Firm varieties like Bosc and Anjou excel in poaching, baking, and roasting (poire), while Bartlett and Comice are ideal fresh, in salads, or paired with artisan cheeses.

## Safety note

Pears contain higher ratios of fructose to glucose as well as sorbitol, a polyol sugar alcohol. Individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), fructose malabsorption, or sensitivity to FODMAPs may experience bloating, abdominal cramps, or osmotic diarrhea upon consuming large quantities. Pear seeds contain minute quantities of cyanogenic glycosides (amygdalin); while accidental ingestion of a few seeds poses no harm, core extraction prior to processing is recommended.

## Sources

- USDA FoodData Central. *Pears, raw, Bartlett (NDB Number: 09252)*. U.S. Department of Agriculture.
- National Institutes of Health (NIH). *Dietary Fiber, Phytochemicals, and Cardiovascular Disease Prevention*. PubMed Central.
- Reiland, H., & Slavin, J. (2015). Systematic Review of Pears and Health Outcomes. *Nutrition Today*, 50(6), 301–305.


========================================================================
FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Accessory Fruits/berry-acc-6.md
========================================================================
---
title: "Apricot: Moorpark, Blenheim, Turkish & Dried — Beta-Carotene & Kernel Controversy"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Apricot: Moorpark, Blenheim, Turkish & Dried — Beta-Carotene & Kernel Controversy."
slug: "berry-acc-6"
category: "Fruits"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
subCategory: "Accessory Fruits"
seoKeywords: ["berry-acc-6", "accessory fruits", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Apricots (*Prunus armeniaca*) are stone fruits (drupes) belonging to the Rosaceae family. Cultivated across heirloom varieties such as Moorpark and Blenheim as well as sun-dried Turkish cultivars, apricots are famed for their vivid orange hue, high beta-carotene density, potassium, dietary fiber, and phenolic antioxidants that support ocular tissue health and mucosal immunity.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Apricots derive their golden-orange flesh from provitamin A carotenoids, dominated by beta-carotene, alpha-carotene, and beta-cryptoxanthin. Beta-carotene undergoes enzymatic cleavage by beta-carotene 15,15'-monooxygenase (BCMO1) in intestinal enterocytes, producing active retinol. Retinol is indispensable for rhodopsin synthesis in retinal rod cells, dark adaptation, and maintaining corneal epithelial integrity.

Fresh and dried apricots contain high concentrations of chlorogenic acid, (+)-catechin, (-)-epicatechin, and rutin. These phenolic compounds attenuate microvascular permeability, protect against ischemia-reperfusion injury, and inhibit lipid peroxidation. Dried apricots concentrate these polyphenols along with dietary potassium, sorbitol, and soluble pectin, fostering gastrointestinal transit and helping maintain vascular compliance.

Micronutrient analysis reveals that a 100-gram serving of fresh apricots delivers over 15% DV for vitamin A and 10% DV for vitamin C, alongside significant copper and potassium. Copper acts as an essential cofactor for cytochrome c oxidase and lysyl oxidase, supporting mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and extracellular collagen/elastin crosslinking.

## Practical notes

Choose plump, firm apricots with a golden-orange skin that yield slightly to gentle thumb pressure. Avoid pale yellow or green-tinged fruit, as well as soft, bruised, or shriveled specimens.

Ripen firm apricots at room temperature (65–70°F / 18–21°C) out of direct sunlight. Once fully ripe, refrigerate at 34–38°F (1–3°C) and consume within 3–5 days.

Wash thoroughly and slice along the suture line to twist open and pop out the pit. Enjoy fresh as a hand fruit, poach gently in honey-lemon syrup, bake into tarts, or add chopped dried apricots to grain salads and Middle Eastern tagines.

## Safety note

Apricot kernels (pits) contain high concentrations of amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside that hydrolyzes in the gastrointestinal tract to release lethal doses of hydrogen cyanide (HCN). Ingesting raw or bitter apricot kernels poses severe cyanide poisoning risks and is strongly discouraged by toxicological agencies. Sulfured dried apricots contain sulfur dioxide, which can trigger severe bronchospasm in asthmatic or sulfite-sensitive individuals.

## Sources

* USDA FoodData Central: Apricots, raw (*Prunus armeniaca*)
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) PubMed: Carotenoid Bioavailability and Health Effects of *Prunus armeniaca*
* European Food Safety Authority (EFSA): Scientific Opinion on Cyanide Risk from Apricot Kernels

FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Aggregate Fruits/berry-agg-1.md

---
title: "Strawberry: June-Bearing, Everbearing, Day-Neutral & Alpine — Fragaria & Fraises"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Strawberry: June-Bearing, Everbearing, Day-Neutral & Alpine — Fragaria & Fraises."
slug: "berry-agg-1"
category: "Fruits"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
subCategory: "Aggregate Fruits"
seoKeywords: ["berry-agg-1", "aggregate fruits", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Strawberries (*Fragaria × ananassa* and *Fragaria vesca*) are botanical accessory-aggregate fruits featuring tiny yellow seed-like achenes embedded on a swollen, sweet floral receptacle. Cultivated across June-bearing, everbearing, day-neutral, and wild alpine varieties, strawberries deliver dense vitamin C, pelargonidin-3-glucoside anthocyanins, folate, manganese, and monomeric ellagitannins for cardiometabolic protection.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Strawberries derive their bright red pigment from pelargonidin-3-glucoside, accompanied by smaller amounts of cyanidin-3-glucoside. Pelargonidin glycosides modulate inflammatory pathways by suppressing lipopolysaccharide-induced expression of interleukin-1 beta (IL-1b) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). Clinical studies demonstrate that consuming 500 grams of fresh strawberries daily for 30 days significantly reduces total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and oxidative biomarkers of lipid peroxidation.

The fruit is an exceptional dietary source of ascorbic acid (vitamin C), providing approximately 58.8 mg per 100g serving—exceeding the vitamin C content of oranges per unit weight. Vitamin C acts as a vital electron donor, regenerating oxidized alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E), supporting collagen triple-helix hydroxylation, and facilitating non-heme iron absorption within the intestinal brush border.

Strawberries also contain significant concentrations of ellagitannins (agrimoniin and pedunculagin), fisetin, and folate (vitamin B9). Fisetin, a senolytic flavonol, selectively induces apoptosis in senescent endothelial and immune cells, reducing systemic low-grade inflammation. Folate supports single-carbon methyl transfer reactions, converting homocysteine to methionine and safeguarding against hyperhomocysteinemia-mediated vascular damage.

## Practical notes

Choose glossy, bright-red strawberries with fresh green calyx caps attached. Avoid strawberries with white or green shoulders, dark soft spots, or dull coloring, as strawberries do not ripen or increase sugar content post-harvest.

Store unwashed in their original ventilated container lined with paper towels in the refrigerator crisper drawer at 34–38°F (1–3°C) for 3–5 days. Keep dry until consumption to prevent mold proliferation.

Hull the green calyx only after washing gently under cool running water. Enjoy whole, sliced into spinach or arugula salads, blended into morning smoothies, dipped in dark chocolate, or macerated briefly with lemon juice.

## Safety note

Strawberries are a frequent cause of IgE-mediated oral allergy syndrome (OAS) in individuals sensitized to birch pollen (*Bet v 1* homolog Fra a 1). White albino strawberry cultivars (*Fra a 1*-deficient) are often tolerated by allergic patients. Additionally, strawberries rank among crops with high pesticide residues, making thorough washing or selecting certified organic options clinically advantageous.

## Sources

* USDA FoodData Central: Strawberries, raw (*Fragaria × ananassa*)
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) PubMed: Strawberry Anthocyanins and Cardiometabolic Health
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin C and Folate Fact Sheets

FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Aggregate Fruits/berry-agg-2.md

---
title: "Raspberry: Red, Black, Golden & Purple — Fragile, Antioxidants & Driscoll’s"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Raspberry: Red, Black, Golden & Purple — Fragile, Antioxidants & Driscoll’s."
slug: "berry-agg-2"
category: "Fruits"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
subCategory: "Aggregate Fruits"
seoKeywords: ["berry-agg-2", "aggregate fruits", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Raspberries (*Rubus idaeus* and *Rubus occidentalis*) are highly delicate aggregate fruits featuring hollow cores created when picked from their central torus. Available in red, black, golden, and purple cultivars, raspberries deliver exceptional levels of ellagitannins, anthocyanins, vitamin C, dietary fiber, and 4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)butan-2-one (raspberry ketone) for cardiovascular and metabolic enhancement.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Raspberries are characterized by high concentrations of sanguiin H-6 and lambertianin C, complex hydrolyzable ellagitannins that yield ellagic acid during GI digestion. Ellagic acid acts as a potent topoisomerase inhibitor and induces apoptosis in abnormal cellular lineages while protecting healthy endothelial cells from oxidative DNA strand breaks. Black raspberries (*R. occidentalis*) offer up to three times the total phenolic and anthocyanin payload of red varieties.

The phenolic profile of raspberries includes cyanidin-3-sophoroside, cyanidin-3-rutinoside, quercetin-3-glucuronide, and tila-roside. Tilaroside, an acylated kaempferol glycoside, acts as a dual PPAR-alpha and PPAR-gamma agonist, promoting fatty acid beta-oxidation in liver and skeletal muscle, blunting adipocyte hypertrophy, and decreasing circulatory triglyceride concentrations.

Delivering 6.5 grams of total dietary fiber per 100-gram serving (over 80% insoluble fiber from seed coats), raspberries yield one of the highest fiber-to-calorie ratios among fresh fruits. Packed with ascorbic acid (providing over 30mg of vitamin C per 100g) and manganese, raspberries bolster extracellular collagen integrity, joint health, and mucosal immunity.

## Practical notes

Choose bright, uniformly colored, plump berries that are completely free of attached hulls (calyx), soft mushy patches, or mold spores. Inspect the bottom of the container for signs of dampness or juice crushing.

Raspberries are extremely perishable and susceptible to *Botrytis cinerea* gray mold. Do not wash prior to storage; keep refrigerated at 34–38°F (1–3°C) in a dry, ventilated container lined with paper towels for a maximum of 2–3 days.

Rinse very gently under a soft stream of cool water immediately before serving. Enjoy raw in berry salads, layer over yogurt or chia pudding, mash into fresh lower-sugar preserves, or purée into smooth coulis for desserts.

## Safety note

Raspberries have been implicated in foodborne outbreaks of *Cyclospora* and *Norovirus* when harvested or handled under unhygienic conditions. Thorough washing under clean potable water is essential. Dietary supplements labeled "raspberry ketones" often contain synthetic compounds at doses far exceeding natural dietary intakes; caution is advised for individuals with cardiovascular conditions or arrhythmia.

## Sources

* USDA FoodData Central: Raspberries, raw (*Rubus idaeus*)
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) PubMed: Ellagitannin Metabolism and Bioactivity of Red and Black Raspberries
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin C Fact Sheet

---
title: "Apple & Pear: Cross-Reference to Berry Section"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Apple & Pear: Cross-Reference to Berry Section."
slug: "pome-ref-1"
category: "Vegetables"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
subCategory: "Already Covered in Berries"
seoKeywords: ["pome-ref-1", "already covered in berries", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Specialty pome fruits—including quince (*Cydonia oblonga*), medlar (*Mespilus germanica*), and loquat (*Eriobotrya japonica*)—belong to the Rosaceae family alongside apples and pears. Characterized by high pectin content, organic acids, and polyphenol polyphenols, these ancient fruits require specific ripening or culinary techniques to soften astringency, yielding substantial dietary fiber, ascorbic acid, and gut-protective polysaccharides.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Quince and medlar contain exceptionally high concentrations of proanthocyanidins, polymeric tannins, and soluble pectin. Raw quince is extremely tart and astringent due to condensed tannins; thermal processing hydrolyzes these tannins while forming a firm gel via pectin cross-linking. Soluble pectin binds dietary cholesterol and bile acids in the intestinal lumen, promoting fecal excretion and assisting lipid homeostasis.

Medlars require a post-harvest softening process known as "bletting"—a controlled fungal-enzymatic breakdown of complex tannins into simple sugars—before becoming palatable. Post-bletting, medlars provide rich amounts of ascorbic acid, malic acid, potassium, and phenolic compounds. Loquats, by contrast, offer high concentrations of beta-carotene, cryptoxanthin, ursolic acid, and triterpenes that support respiratory lining health and suppress oxidative stress.

Phytochemical studies on quince seed mucilage and loquat extracts show significant anti-inflammatory and gastroprotective activity. Quince seeds yield hydrocolloid polysaccharides that coat esophageal and gastric mucous membranes, relieving symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux and ulceration, while loquat leaf triterpenes exhibit bronchodilatory effects in preclinical respiratory models.

## Practical notes

Select firm, fragrant yellow quinces free from deep blemishes. Choose plump, orange loquats that yield slightly to pressure. Select firm medlars and allow them to blet at room temperature until brown and soft.

Quince and loquat store well under refrigeration at 34–38°F (1–3°C) for 2–3 weeks. Medlars should be stored stem-side down on straw or cardboard at cool ambient temperatures during the bletting process.

Cook quince by poaching in water with honey, baking into tarts, or simmering into Spanish *membrillo* (quince paste). Peel and seed loquats to enjoy fresh or in jams. Eat bletted medlars raw by scooping out the soft, spiced-apple-like pulp.

## Safety note

Seeds of quince, loquat, and medlar contain cyanogenic glycosides (primarily amygdalin). While accidental ingestion of a few intact seeds is typically harmless, crushing, chewing, or consuming large quantities of pome seeds can release toxic hydrogen cyanide and should be strictly avoided.

## Sources

* USDA FoodData Central: Quince, raw (*Cydonia oblonga*)
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) PubMed: Pectin and Bioactive Compounds of *Cydonia oblonga* and *Eriobotrya japonica*
* European Food Safety Authority (EFSA): Evaluation of Cyanogenic Glycosides in Rosaceae Fruit Seeds

title: "Watermelon, Cantaloupe, Honeydew & Specialty Melons: Cross-Reference to Vegetables"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Watermelon, Cantaloupe, Honeydew & Specialty Melons: Cross-Reference to Vegetables."
slug: "melon-ref-1"
category: "Fruits"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
subCategory: "Already Covered in Cucurbits"
seoKeywords: ["melon-ref-1", "already covered in cucurbits", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Melons—comprising watermelon (*Citrullus lanatus*), cantaloupe (*Cucumis melo* var. *cantalupensis*), and honeydew (*Cucumis melo* inodorus group)—belong to the botanical family Cucurbitaceae. While taxonomically related to squashes and cucumbers, their culinary and dietary roles emphasize refreshing dessert hydration, delivering concentrated lycopene, beta-carotene, L-citrulline, ascorbic acid, and essential electrolytes for vascular function and athletic recovery.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Watermelon is one of nature's richest sources of red lycopene, providing even higher bioavailable concentrations per unit weight than raw red tomatoes. Lycopene neutralizes singlet oxygen and attenuates oxidative damage in arterial walls, mitigating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) oxidation. Furthermore, watermelon flesh and rind are packed with L-citrulline, an amino acid precursor to L-arginine, which drives endothelial nitric oxide synthesis, reduces muscle soreness, and improves exercise performance.

Orange-fleshed cantaloupes provide exceptional provitamin A carotenoids, with a 100-gram serving satisfying nearly 100% of daily vitamin A requirements. Beta-carotene supports cellular differentiation, immune surveillance, and cutaneous photo-protection against solar radiation. Honeydew melons add significant amounts of vitamin C, folate, and potassium, aiding intracellular fluid balance and arterial compliance.

Composed of over 90% structured cellular water, melons serve as excellent physiological rehydration agents. The synergistic combination of soluble carbohydrates, potassium, and magnesium facilitates rapid gastrointestinal fluid absorption without triggering gastric distress or osmotic overload.

## Practical notes

Choose watermelons with a creamy yellow field spot and a dull, hollow thumping sound. For cantaloupe and honeydew, select heavy fruits with a sweet floral aroma at the blossom end and slight yield to gentle pressure.

Store whole uncut melons at room temperature (around 55–70°F / 13–21°C) for up to 1–2 weeks. Once sliced, cover tightly or place in airtight containers and refrigerate at 34–38°F (1–3°C) for 3–4 days.

Scrub outer rinds thoroughly under cold running water before cutting to prevent transferring surface bacteria into the flesh. Enjoy fresh in fruit salads, paired with salty feta cheese and mint, blended into chilled agua frescas, or frozen into natural sorbets.

## Safety note

Cantaloupe outer rinds have textured netting that can harbor foodborne pathogens such as *Listeria monocytogenes* and *Salmonella*. Always wash the exterior thoroughly prior to slicing. Individuals with severe chronic kidney disease (CKD) should monitor total portion sizes due to cantaloupe's high potassium content.

## Sources

* USDA FoodData Central: Watermelon, raw (*Citrullus lanatus*)
* USDA FoodData Central: Melons, cantaloupe, raw (*Cucumis melo*)
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) PubMed: L-Citrulline Supplementation and Vascular Nitric Oxide Bioavailability

FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Asian Leafy Greens/leaf-asia-4.md

---
title: "Malabar Spinach: Basella alba, Red & Green, Mucilaginous & Heat-Loving"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Malabar Spinach: Basella alba, Red & Green, Mucilaginous & Heat-Loving."
slug: "leaf-asia-4"
category: "Vegetables"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
subCategory: "Asian Leafy Greens"
seoKeywords: ["leaf-asia-4", "asian leafy greens", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Malabar spinach (Basella alba and Basella rubra) is a heat-tolerant, mucilaginous tropical vine widely cultivated across Asia and Africa. Distinct from true spinach, it thrives during hot summer months and yields fleshy, succulent leaves packed with bioavailable carotenoids, ascorbic acid, dietary fiber, and essential minerals for cardiovascular and gastrointestinal wellness.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Malabar spinach features impressive concentrations of provitamin A carotenoids (beta-carotene and lutein) alongside vitamin C and folate. A 100-gram serving supplies over 100% of the Daily Value for vitamin A, supporting ocular tissue integrity, epithelial barrier defense, and immune cell differentiation. The red-stemmed variety (*Basella rubra*) contains betalain pigments, potent nitrogen-containing antioxidants that scavenge free radicals and mitigate oxidative lipid peroxidation in vascular endothelium.

Botanically distinguished by its high mucilage content, *Basella* leaves yield soluble polysaccharides that form a protective hydrocolloid barrier across the gastric mucosa. This mucilage slows carbohydrate absorption, blunting postprandial glucose spikes, and promotes favorable short-chain fatty acid production through colonic fermentation. Additionally, the green stems deliver substantial non-heme iron, magnesium, calcium, and potassium, which together support bone density maintenance and electrolyte balance.

Clinical research indicates that polyphenolic extracts from Malabar spinach exhibit anti-inflammatory activity by downregulating pro-inflammatory cytokine expression (TNF-alpha and IL-6). The combination of dietary fiber, saponins, and phytosterols enhances fecal bile acid excretion, supporting healthy lipid profiles and protecting against metabolic syndrome.

## Practical notes

Select crisp, dark green or dark purple-stemmed leaves without wilting, yellowing, or dark water-soaked spots. Thick, succulent leaves indicate peak freshness.

Wrap unwashed leaves loosely in a damp paper towel and store in a perforated plastic bag in the refrigerator crisper drawer at 34–38°F (1–3°C) for up to 4–5 days.

Rinse thoroughly in cold running water to remove grit. Young leaves can be eaten raw in salads, while mature leaves and tender stems excel in stir-fries, curries, and soups, where the natural mucilage acts as a comforting, nutrient-rich thickener.

## Safety note

Malabar spinach contains moderate levels of soluble oxalates. Individuals with a history of calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis (kidney stones) or hyperoxaluria should moderate their intake and consume it blanched or cooked alongside adequate hydration. Due to its mild laxative properties from high mucilage, rapid increase in consumption may cause transient loose stools.

## Sources

* USDA FoodData Central: Malabar Spinach, raw (*Basella alba*)
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin A and Carotenoids Fact Sheet
* National Institutes of Health (NIH) PubMed: Phytochemical and Pharmacological Profile of *Basella alba*

FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Asian Leafy Greens/leaf-asia-5.md

title: "Kangkong/Water Spinach: Ipomoea aquatica, Hollow Stems & Southeast Asian"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Kangkong/Water Spinach: Ipomoea aquatica, Hollow Stems & Southeast Asian."
slug: "leaf-asia-5"
category: "Vegetables"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
subCategory: "Asian Leafy Greens"
seoKeywords: ["leaf-asia-5", "asian leafy greens", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Kangkong (*Ipomoea aquatica*), or water spinach, is a semi-aquatic tropical green vegetable widely cultivated throughout Southeast Asia. Featuring hollow succulent stems and tender arrow-shaped leaves, kangkong provides extraordinary concentrations of beta-carotene, ascorbic acid, iron, and flavonoids. Thorough cooking enhances digestibility and eliminates potential aquatic parasite vectors while supporting glycemic regulation and hepatic antioxidant defenses.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Kangkong is a rich source of provitamin A carotenoids, notably beta-carotene and lutein, delivering over 200% of the daily value per 100 g serving. Beta-carotene undergoes enzymatic cleavage by beta-carotene 15,15'-monooxygenase in intestinal enterocytes to form active retinal, supporting epithelial membrane repair, immune cell differentiation, and ocular rhodopsin regeneration. Additionally, high ascorbic acid levels act synergistically with dietary non-heme iron to optimize iron absorption in the gut.

Phytochemically, *Ipomoea aquatica* contains abundant phenolic acids (chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid, and ferulic acid) and flavonoids (quercetin, myricetin, and kaempferol glycosides). Preclinical and clinical investigations show that kangkong extracts possess significant insulin-mimetic and hypoglycemic properties. Flavonoids in kangkong inhibit intestinal alpha-glucosidase and enhance peripheral glucose uptake in skeletal muscle, aiding in postprandial glycemic control.

Moreover, kangkong delivers key electrolytes and minerals including potassium, calcium, magnesium, and dietary fiber. Its soluble fiber fraction binds intestinal bile acids and delays gastric emptying, promoting satiety and supporting systemic lipid homeostasis. The antioxidant polyphenol network reduces lipid peroxidation in hepatic parenchymal tissues.

## Practical notes

Select kangkong with bright green, crisp leaves and firm, hollow stems; avoid shoots showing yellowing, wilting, or black slimy spots. Because kangkong grows in semi-aquatic marshlands, leaves and stems can accumulate mud and aquatic flora. Wash thoroughly under cold running water multiple times. Separate tender leaves from thick stems, adding stems to stir-fries slightly before leaves. Kangkong is classically stir-fried over high heat with garlic, chilies, soy sauce, or fermented shrimp paste (belacan).

## Safety note

Raw or undercooked kangkong harvested from wild aquatic habitats can transmit *Fasciolopsis buski*, a giant intestinal fluke parasite encysted on water plants. Thorough cooking (boiling or stir-frying to >100°C) completely kills parasite metacercariae, ensuring safe consumption. Furthermore, due to its invasive growth habit, cultivation is regulated in certain US states (such as Florida and Texas).

## Sources

- USDA FoodData Central: Water spinach, raw (FDC ID: 169280)
- National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Dietary Supplements: Vitamin A and Iron Fact Sheets
- NIH National Library of Medicine (PubMed): Hypoglycemic and Antioxidant Effects of Ipomoea aquatica

FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Asparagus & Artichokes/stalk-1.md

title: "Asparagus: Green, White, Purple & Wild — Spring King, Urine & Antiquity"
description: "Clinical overview, safety guidelines, and evidence-graded applications for Asparagus: Green, White, Purple & Wild — Spring King, Urine & Antiquity."
slug: "stalk-1"
category: "Vegetables"
author: "NutritionColours Editorial Team"
reviewedBy: "Dr. Shilpa Thakur"
lastUpdated: 2026-07-14
subCategory: "Asparagus & Artichokes"
seoKeywords: ["stalk-1", "asparagus & artichokes", "clinical protocol", "nutrition"]
---

## Overview

Asparagus (*Asparagus officinalis*) is a perennial spring vegetable prized across green, white, purple, and wild varieties. Delivering abundant folate, phylloquinone, glutathione, and prebiotic inulin, asparagus exerts clinical benefits on renal diuresis, cellular detoxification, and vascular endothelial protection. Its characteristic post-ingestion urinary odor stems from S-methylmethionine metabolic degradation into volatile sulfur metabolites.

## Nutrition & Phytochemistry

Asparagus is an outstanding source of dietary folate (vitamin B9), supplying over 60% of the recommended daily intake per cooked cup (180 g). Folate serves as an essential coenzyme in one-carbon transfer reactions, driving nucleic acid synthesis and regulating homocysteine methylation. Elevated plasma homocysteine is an established risk factor for cardiovascular disease and vascular dementia; regular consumption of folate-dense asparagus helps maintain physiological homocysteine concentrations.

Phytochemically, asparagus contains high levels of asparagusic acid (1,2-dithiolane-4-carboxylic acid) and its derivatives, unique sulfur-containing organosulfur molecules. Upon human digestion, asparagusic acid metabolizes into volatile sulfur compounds, predominantly methanethiol, dimethyl sulfide, and dimethyl disulfide. These volatile odorants are rapidly excreted by the kidneys into urine. Furthermore, asparagus provides abundant saponins (protodioscin and sarsasapogenin) and flavonoids (quercetin and rutin), which demonstrate antihypertensive activity by inhibiting angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and reducing capillary fragility.

Additionally, asparagus supplies substantial reduced glutathione (GSH), one of the body's primary endogenous tripeptide antioxidants, alongside phylloquinone (vitamin K1), ascorbic acid, and potassium. Potassium promotes renal natriuresis, aiding in blood pressure regulation, while glutathione scavenges free radicals and assists Phase II hepatic detoxification enzymes.

## Practical notes

Select asparagus spears with firm, straight stalks and tightly closed, compact tips; avoid spears that appear limp, woody, or dry at the cut ends. Store fresh asparagus upright with the cut ends submerged in an inch of water in the refrigerator, loosely covered with a plastic bag, for up to four days. To prepare, gently bend each stalk near the bottom until it snaps at its natural break point between the tender upper stalk and woody base. Roast with olive oil at high temperatures, steam briefly, or slice raw into ribbon salads.

## Safety note

Asparagus is high in purines, which metabolize into uric acid; individuals with hyperuricemia or acute gouty arthritis should consume asparagus in moderate amounts. Individuals receiving vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant therapy (e.g., warfarin) must maintain consistent daily intakes of asparagus to prevent fluctuations in therapeutic anticoagulation parameters.

## Sources

- USDA FoodData Central: Asparagus, cooked, boiled, drained (FDC ID: 168390)
- National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Dietary Supplements: Folate Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
- NIH National Library of Medicine (PubMed): Asparagusic Acid Metabolism, Saponins, and Health Applications of Asparagus officinalis

FILE: foods/MiscBotanical/Asparagus & Artichokes/stalk-2.md
